Katalog Berita (Halaman 27/57)

#6062. KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us. The crew followed a rule exactly, and as far as I can tell, nobody got anything out of it.

Business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked. On some planes the middle seat is physically blocked with a small table. On this flight it was just empty, blocked online so nobody could book it, but technically a regular seat anyone could sit in.

I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.

After the doors closed, it turned out that two passengers had boarding passes for the same seat. Whoever got there first sat down. The other one was a fairly young guy, and now he had nowhere to sit. The flight was completely full, there wasn’t a single free seat in economy.

I heard the crew apologizing to him and saying they would have to take him off the plane and put him on the next flight.

I knew this would take a while, because the doors were already closed and he had boarded. Getting him off meant opening the doors again, and maybe taking his bag off too. Once on another flight someone got off and everyone had to hold up their bags.

And I felt sorry for the guy. Maybe he was in a hurry to get somewhere, and none of this was his fault. The airline gave two people boarding passes for one seat, and he was already on board.

So I asked my wife if she minded giving up the empty seat between us. The flight is only about two hours. She was fine with it, so I went to the crew and offered it.

The crew was very grateful, but said seating someone there was against the rules and they couldn’t decide it themselves, they had to check with someone.

That took about 10 minutes. Then they came back, thanked me again, and said that unfortunately it wasn’t possible under the rules.

So they opened the doors and offloaded the guy, I hope they rebooked him on the next one. In the end we pushed back about 40 minutes late and landed in Barcelona about half an hour late. After landing I think even the captain came over, shook my hand and thanked me.

As I understand it, the middle seat is blocked to give the business class passengers more space. In this case that was us, and we were the ones offering to give that space up.

We didn’t need the space, and we’d have put up with one more person in the row for two hours.

On a completely full KLM flight, two passengers got boarding passes for the same seat. My wife and I offered the empty blocked seat between us in business, so he wouldn’t have to get off. The crew checked with someone, the answer was no, and he was offloaded anyway, and we left about 40 minutes late.

I get that the crew couldn’t make this call themselves. Still, we didn’t need that seat at all.

Is there a good reason for this rule that I’m missing?

I suspect unfortunately this was one of those situations where "the rules are the rules," and that's that, and it might've literally been a system limitation. Perhaps they couldn't figure out how to technically show someone as being "loaded" on the flight, given that the middle seats don't have a corresponding seat in the system. As far as the GDS knows, those middle seats aren't blocked, but instead, they just don't exist. But you're of course absolutely right, in the end there was a substantial delay, and this could've been avoided.

Mendocino, a small coastal town in northern California, has welcomed its first points property. The nearly 50-year-old Hill House hotel was renovated and reopened in June 2026 as Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy — making it the first and only member of a major hotel loyalty program in Mendocino proper. (The closest options are members of IHG One Rewards and Wyndham Rewards in neighboring Fort Bragg.)

The Mendocino Coast region is known for its charming small-town vibes, natural beauty and outdoor pursuits, so the Trailborn brand’s laidback nature lodge concept fits in here like a seal in nearby Mendocino Bay. I stayed three nights in late October to get a first look at the property (and the town, which is on TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list).

Nestled just a few minutes’ walk outside downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino’s unassuming two-story buildings fit right in with the surrounding hotel scene. The design is inspired by nature — specifically, the redwood forests and tide pools of the surrounding Mendocino Coast — while still feeling modern and polished.

The grounds are bursting with native plants, many of them still in bloom when I visited in late October. Botanical art prints and zoological illustrations on the walls give a nod to the great outdoors, and curious guests can lose themselves in the lobby’s curiosity cabinet, a revamped relic of the original building. Visitors are encouraged to sign the guestbook with a stamp of a dried leaf or flower.

The hotel offers just 44 accommodations — relatively large for a Mendocino property — including 14 double queen rooms, 25 king rooms and 5 junior suites. Within each room type, travelers can choose to upgrade to features such as a balcony or deck, an ocean view or both.

My room, a spacious King Junior Suite Ocean View, felt like a relaxing retreat with its muted color palette of greens, browns and yellows and its cozy linen spa robes. After a day of exploring Mendocino, I enjoyed relaxing on the sofa, perusing the coffee table book Botanicum, and sampling locally made goodies from the snack basket and minibar (for a fee).

Trailborn Hill House has one on-site restaurant: Pizza Standard Time, a casual bar and diner offering mostly pizza, plus salads, charcuterie boards and small Italian bites like arancini. The fare was limited but tasty; my friend and I tried a pizza, salad, and local Husch chardonnay and were quite happy. It’s nice having a quick, casual meal available on-site in case you arrive late and tired from the drive, but it’s also just a few minutes’ walk to Mendocino if you want more options.

Like all Trailborn properties, this one offers a lobby convenience store called Hill House Wine & Grocer. Guests can purchase local drinks and snacks (mostly the kind you’d find on a charcuterie board), plus apparel, toys, candles with the property’s signature scent and other souvenirs.

The hotel also offered a small but delicious complimentary breakfast spread. As with everything else during my stay, the breakfast was high-quality yet unpretentious, with guests serving and bussing their own tables. Instead of having a designated breakfast area, guests can find a cozy spot to eat inside Pizza Standard Time or the attached Cabot Cove Detective Library, outside by one of the fire pits or back to their room.

However, this will change when Trailborn’s second Mendocino property, The Mendocino Hotel, opens in 2027. Instead of complimentary breakfast, Hill House plans to provide guests with a voucher to Moonwave, The Mendocino Hotel’s dining concept, which will serve “coastal comfort” food three meals a day plus drinks at the lobby bar.

If you didn’t realize you were in a small town, you will as soon as you interact with any of the hotel staff — everyone I spoke to, from front desk staff to custodians, was beyond friendly.

As for amenities, they align with the brand’s laid-back, outdoorsy style and with some of the things the Mendocino area is known for. You’ll find:

Located just a few minutes’ walk (or bike ride) from downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn puts guests in the heart of the town’s charming boutiques and varied dining and drinking scene. But you won’t get bored if you hang around the property, either.

Here are some of the on-site activities guests may want to try:

While Mendocino’s remoteness makes it a haven for crowd-weary travelers, it’s becoming easier than ever to reach thanks to recent roadwork funding and new direct flights to Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), including on Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest. That’s one reason Mendo made TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list.

But travelers can also fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC), which are a bit farther away but offer more flight options.

Depending on the airport you choose, you’ll need to rent a car and drive two to four hours to Mendocino.

Basic rooms start as low as $140 per night in the off-season, while my King Junior Suite Ocean View starts around $350 per night (though these prices can climb much higher on summer weekends). Award rates start at 48,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night, or you could redeem a 50,000-point free night certificate.

When booking, you’ll want to use one of the credit cards that earn the most points for Marriott stays, as well as one that possibly offers automatic Marriott Bonvoy elite status for value-added benefits. These include:

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hill House has three wheelchair-accessible rooms, including two double queens and one king; these feature accessible tubs and, in some cases, roll-in showers. The property and its parking lot are also wheelchair accessible. For hearing-impaired guests, a portable kit can be installed in any room.

As a points traveler who loves Mendocino, I’m thrilled to see the town’s first points property not only opening but thriving. As a traveler who appreciates unique stays and has experienced some of the town’s charming independent properties, I’m also glad that Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino has brought enough character to fit seamlessly into the local scene.

It seems the Trailborn brand — and Marriott Bonvoy — is betting big on Mendocino. Hill House is one of two Mendocino properties purchased by The Trailborn brand. The second, the 150-year-old Mendocino Hotel, is undergoing renovation and slated to open in 2027.

#6060. Malaysia Airlines Orders Up To 16 Boeing 787-10s, Deliveries Start 2032

Malaysia Airlines has just placed a new aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

The oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:

“The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”

For context, Malaysia Airlines currently has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:

Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:

A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

The big challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can…

Malaysia Airlines is the newest customer for the Boeing 787, as the airline has ordered up to 16 787-10s, including 10 firm orders and six options. The airline plans to use this for a long haul expansion to Europe, as well as for flights in Asia-Pacific.

It’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines continuing to grow, as the carrier has quite the order book at this point. I am curious if the airline keeps around the seven A350s in the long run, or how the airline manages its three wide body aircraft types.

What do you make of Malaysia Airlines’ Boeing 787-10 order?

#6059. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

"When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

“The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”

That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”

A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

“We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

#6058. A George Floyd Musical: What Could Go Wrong?

The serious issues underneath an unserious moral panic

Demonstrators hold signs depicting George Floyd during a protest against police brutality and racial inequality in Brooklyn, N.Y., June 13, 2020.

Playbill, a site for all things theater-related, posted a job listing seeking “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record George Floyd: The Musical, a new project by the Busted Broadway group based in New Jersey that “exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary.” On its website, the group’s tagline for the show is “The $20 Bill That Changed the World!”

Playbill has since released an apology claiming it “incorrectly approved” the job posting for its site, and is now reviewing its internal processes. “We know this listing has upset and offended many, and the fact that it made it onto our site has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet. For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement reads. In response to the post, some people have demanded that Playbill take more accountability by explaining exactly how such a thing was approved for the site, expose who is behind the musical (though that was already public), hire more minorities to prevent similar wrongdoing in the future, and issue apologies to the Floyd family and the black community. Others have more firmly called for barring the musical’s creative leader from the platform entirely.

Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

#6056. SkyWest Pilots Do The Right Thing At SFO, Then Get Snapped At By ATC

With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness. So along those lines, here’s a case of a pilot paying close attention to ensure everyone’s safety, and then an air traffic controller being frustrated by that…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX). The pilots were switched to the ground frequency, and that’s when things quickly went downhill:

The SkyWest pilots then continued their taxi, and when they got to the gate, the conversation continued:

When you screw up, I suppose it’s human nature to get a bit defensive, and I think that’s exactly what happened here.

Credit to the SkyWest pilots for their situational awareness here. They were instructed to taxi in front of another plane, and another plane was instructed to give way to them, but never read back those instructions. The air traffic controller absolutely should have caught that, and as a pilot, they 100% did the correct thing by noticing the lack of a read back, and erring on the side of caution.

This isn’t just some theoretical risk, but ground collisions are the most common kinds of accidents involving commercial aircraft. Could the SkyWest pilots have said “we’re holding short because the other plane didn’t read back instructions?” Sure, but it seems like the time gap here was a matter of seconds, and they didn’t want to step on the radio calls of another pilot, in case they were going to read back.

What I think is really unprofessional is how the air traffic controller then responded to this:

The pilots of a SkyWest flight decided to hold short of a taxiway after they observed the plane that was supposed to give way to them not reading back the correct instructions. That was absolutely the right move, and the air traffic controller should’ve caught that.

#6054. Why JetBlue Is My Favorite Way To Fly Economy Across The Atlantic

I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy. JetBlue definitely stands out as being my favorite, and dare I say it, the most premium of all the transatlantic economy flights I’ve experienced.

My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location. The airline covered my flights for the event, but had no input in this article. I’d like to share some of the reasons that JetBlue’s transatlantic experience impressed me so much.

Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.

JetBlue currently partners with NYC-based Dig Inn for its transatlantic economy-class meals, and they’re far better than average. They also offer products from a range of interesting brands, rather than just your classic soda labels.

Here’s an example of the drinks menu on my flight from Amsterdam to Boston.

Meals are served in these stylish, reusable, matte-black sealed containers. I’d love to see more airlines do more to reduce their waste like this.

I was very happy with my choice of chicken pesto pasta salad as the main course, accompanied by sides of beet and carrot slaw and snap peas with feta. The fresh, flavorful, yet cold dishes were far better than many of the reheated slop I’ve been served in economy before.

I was equally impressed by the breakfast I had on the morning departure back from Boston to London Heathrow (LHR). I went for the Bubly sparkling water again, as I avoid coffee on a plane unless it’s served as espresso. The stuff they pour out of those vats is pretty much just glorified dirty water.

As far as pre-landing light meals go, this pizza thing was pretty good, too.

In addition to the main meal and pre-landing light bite, JetBlue keeps a well-stocked pantry at the back of the Airbus A321LR.

JetBlue has been offering fast, free, in-flight Wi-Fi for as long as I can remember. The same cannot be said for some full-service carriers, which still can’t guarantee a reliable, fast, and free connection on their transatlantic flights.

They’ve also added some fun tech features, like the ability to choose the elements for the main meal service via the IFE screen, even in economy. I think it has a more premium feel than being asked “chicken or beef?”

I’m not a frequent JetBlue flyer, so I couldn’t really make the most of the fun personalization features, such as the option to continue watching the movie where you left off on your last flight.

Being given anything more than the standard pillow and blanket in economy is a rare bonus. It had been so long since my last JetBlue flight in economy that I’d forgotten about the complimentary Snooze Kit.

I prefer to use my AirPods to earplugs, but I did make good use of the eye mask for a mid-flight nap.

I’ve flown over my fair share of narrow bodies on long-haul flights, and I genuinely don’t know why such a fuss is made about them being terrible.

JetBlue’s version of the aircraft has comfy seats, with standard Core (economy) seats having 32 inches of pitch. Another common complaint I hear is that there are fewer toilets. For a plane with far fewer passengers (only 114 in economy), fewer toilets kind of makes sense. I didn’t once find myself waiting in line to use the bathroom on either flight.

For what it’s worth, there are two lavatories for 114 economy passengers, so that’s one lavatory per 57 passengers. That’s a little lower than the industry standard, but not by much. For example, American’s standard 787-9s have five lavatories for 255 economy seats, so that’s a ratio of one lavatory per 51 passengers.

If you’ve only got the budget or the points for economy for your next trip to Europe, I couldn’t recommend JetBlue more. They now fly to eight cities in Europe, the planes are comfortable and modern, and the in-flight food and beverage is top of the game for economy.

What do you make of JetBlue’s transatlantic economy offering?

#6053. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

“I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

“I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

“Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”

Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

“I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”

Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”

“We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

“That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

“There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”

It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

“My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

“The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”

That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

“I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

#6052. British Airways Visa Card Review: Is It Worth The $95 Annual Fee?

The British Airways Visa Signature® Card is one of Chase’s co-branded airline credit cards, and British Airways Club is certainly a popular frequent flyer program, given the overall value of the Avios ecosystem, plus the number of destinations in the United States that British Airways serves.

Who should be applying for the British Airways Visa, and under what circumstances is it worth spending money on it? Let’s take a look at what you need to know about this card, and what the best alternatives are.

Link: Learn more about the British Airways Visa Signature® Card

Before jumping into a closer look at every aspect of the British Airways Visa Card, here’s a high-level view of the card’s key features, perks, and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the biggest British Airways Visa Card pros and cons:

If you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these important details.

The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized users.

British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

The British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

The British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:

There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

There are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:

British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

Often one of the big challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get the card in a household, etc.

There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

One of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

If you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:

There are some basic terms to be aware of:

British Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa companion voucher.

As a Visa Signature card, the British Airways Visa comes with the following shopping and travel protection benefits:

You’ll want to review the card’s benefits guide for any exclusions and rules that apply.

The British Airways Visa Card has a solid welcome bonus, and that could be a legitimate motivator for picking up this card. However, personally this isn’t a card I would use for everyday spending, since you can earn British Airways Avios at a better rate with other American Express or Chase cards. It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:

#6051. Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,…

So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

#6050. What We Leave Out When We Talk About Sexism in Science

The research on bias against women in STEM is far more mixed than the headlines suggest.

Imagine you’re a young woman considering a career in science. You’ve heard that when a man and a woman with identical qualifications apply for the same job, hiring committees tend to favor the man. You ask for evidence, and someone sends you a study. It’s a real study, published in a prestigious journal, and it says more or less what you were told. Case closed?

Steve Stewart-Williams is a professor of psychology at the University of Nottingham Malaysia.

The Norway-based long-haul budget airline said in a statement early Thursday that all flights were suspended "pending clarification as to whether a viable financing solution can be established."

"There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," Norse added.

The confirmation followed the cancellation of all Norse flights late on Wednesday, the flight tracking website FlightRadar24 shows.

Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, said Wednesday evening on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice."

Norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

During the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

At its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

The collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

Norse warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical" and said its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs."

Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

Story updated with Norse confirmation of its shut down.

#6047. Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)

Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes…

At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf

WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m

Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v

This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。…

Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1

A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97

It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”

A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP

It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots.

While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists.

It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be.

Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉

A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers.

Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great.

What do you make of this FedEx MD-11 accident in Miami?

#6046. At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

“I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”

Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

New leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

#6045. The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing. This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare.

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before. For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion.

Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in.

Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate.

The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays. Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows:

How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate.

Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate.

What do you make of this Park Hyatt Beaver Creek promotion?

#6044. Huang’s Surprise Return Doesn’t End Nvidia Questions

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026.

Well, that was quick. Less than two weeks after unanimously accepting CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board has now, again unanimously, agreed to reinstate him. This followed “a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” The first hurdle must have been trickier than the second. Presumably even more importantly, based on “input” from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, the board was “confident” that Huang’s return posed “no national security risk.”

President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation. In a post on Truth Social, he argued that it was needed “in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy.”

On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars. The tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 6.5 percent, the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent. Trump views the stock market as a critical indicator of the nation’s economic health, not without reason, including the “wealth effect” created by rising stock prices. Booms can go bust, but, although calculating the effect of the AI build-out on the economy is not straightforward, by some estimates it may account for a quarter or more of current GDP growth.

Trump also wrote that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Huang’s “return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump added that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of [its] compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect U.S. national security.” And so it should.

Various government agencies are investigating, as are a number of congressional committees. It was also announced on Monday that the U.S. is prohibiting the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm previously connected to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Nvidia’s CEO was in a relationship. The concern is that Megaspeed may have been diverting contraband chips to China. More generally, the administration has already tightened the rules governing exports of such chips to other countries where there is a diversion risk, a welcome, if overdue, step, as is the closing of the loophole that allowed enterprises in China and other hostile states to have remote access to the power of advanced American AI chips from businesses located in third countries.

This is a saga with a lot to unpack, much of which remains, at best, guesswork. Nevertheless, we do know (or can be pretty sure that) Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang considerable leeway when it came to the way he ran Nvidia, not least with regard to the way that so much of the company’s decision-making was concentrated in him. That may well have underpinned Nvidia’s extraordinary success — a win for the U.S., as well as for Nvidia — but it also clearly played an important part in the current imbroglio and raises troubling questions about the consequences were Huang to step down again or, even if he weathers this crisis, at some later stage. It is said that no man is irreplaceable, but that is not always so.

We also know that Nvidia, sometimes referred to as AI’s central bank, has played a key role in supporting the growth of earlier-stage companies. This has been criticized as a form of circular financing by Nvidia (the company is helping fund some of its client base), but it has played a vital part in the creation of an American AI ecosystem. Through Nvidia, Huang was a critical element in this ecosystem’s growth.

And we know that the success of the American AI sector has geopolitical as well as commercial implications. There is an AI race between China and the U.S. The U.S. must hang on to the lead it has built up — here’s the catch — in no small part with Nvidia’s assistance. Huang has argued against overly broad U.S. restrictions on the export of U.S. chips, arguing that they will only encourage China to make their own, an unconvincing argument given the importance Beijing puts on autarky. Of course, Nvidia would benefit financially (for a while) by selling AI chips to China, but it is not in our strategic interest to allow it.

Huang is entitled to his views, but they do not entitle his company to evade U.S, export controls or even to turn a blind eye should Nvidia’s customers “divert” chips to forbidden destinations. The question of whether this occurred will almost certainly be the main focus of the investigations. It is a question that dwarfs (however much corporate governance purists may object) Huang’s reckless choice of companionship and, in this respect, his lack of candor with Nvidia’s board. The investigations will lead where they will lead. They will also be highly politicized. Regardless of the investigations’ conclusions, they will be a major distraction and, as such, unhelpful to Nvidia and the U.S. AI sector more broadly. That will be a win that should never have been handed to Beijing.
