#6025. GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

“I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

Democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

Ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”

At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

“It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”

Democrats said Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

Democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

“First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he said. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”

Peters said when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

“We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”

Ueland said his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

Ueland said he would give it a “medium grade over time.”

For example, he said GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”

By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”

Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

Ueland said he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”

Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, said he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”

“For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

Paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

“We see that bipartisan process as extremely important to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” said Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, said by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”

He said GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”

The union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

#6022. FedEx Jet Runs Off Miami Runway 80 Days After Amazon Air Crash Killed 5 There

FedEx flight 910 from Memphis ran off the end of runway 26R at Miami airport Wednesday night and stopped in the grass just inside the fence at NW 67th Avenue. From across the street, the nose of the MD-11 lined up with the traffic light. Both people aboard got out safely. Nobody on the ground was hurt. Eighty days earlier, a Boeing 767 flying for Amazon Air crossed that same avenue after landing on a different runway. Five people in a van died. Here’s how close the FedEx jet came to the street on Thanksgiving eve, in a photo shared by aviation watchdog JonNYC. FedEx off the runway at Miami https://t.co/WouB3hu13t — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 26, 2026 The plane landed at 8:26 p.m. Eastern. On the tower recording, the FedEx crew calls in to report they’ve gone off the runway. “We see it,” comes the reply. Then the controller turns to another airplane. “American 2199, go around.” Moments later, the controller gives a different American Airlines crew instructions to taxi off the parallel runway. Listen to Miami tower and FedEx 910, and see the flight track. The aircraft was N605FE, named April Star. Here it is at Frankfurt in 2008, via Kambui (CC BY 2.0). Miami had one runway available. The FAA held Miami-bound flights at their departure airports, and its subsequent delay program projected an average wait of 3 hours and 34 minutes for arrivals. At 10:30 p.m. the airport reopened the diagonal runway for departures. The south runway was handling both takeoffs and landings. What A Miami Controller Reported Before FedEx Landed Reporter Anna Giaritelli says a Miami air traffic controller sent her a text before the overrun, while the controller was off duty. They described aircraft headed for Miami and Fort Lauderdale running out of routes around the weather, landlines going down between facilities and more than 10 reports of severe turbulence. “This was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen.” Read the controller’s message and see the regional weather radar. The FAA’s 6 p.m. operations plan shows thunderstorms made Atlantic routes unusable. Miami Center wanted departures routed down the middle of Florida, and controllers had to leave extra space between planes they handed off to Havana because of a communications problem. By 7:43 p.m., the FAA said the Havana equipment problem was resolved. One Boeing 767 crew reported severe turbulence at 8,000 feet about 39 nautical miles south of Miami at 4:24 p.m. At the airport there was light rain, seven miles of visibility and a south wind at 6 knots gusting to 18. Twelve minutes after Fedex landed, the airport reported thunderstorms to the northeast and east. Watch the roadside video of the two aircraft. #6021. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

The "big four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

"This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito said before passage.

Ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, plan and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as currently drafted.

However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an issue: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the new Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

Merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

Some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

"I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley said before the vote Thursday night.

But Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental issues under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

After decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

Flight cancellations quickly climbed on Thanksgiving Day as a coastal storm put a damper on holiday travel — and festivities — up and down the East Coast.

Heavy rain and wind fueled flight cancellations at several of the nation's busiest hubs. And the flight woes were at risk to worsen as the storm system tracked north.

Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI) saw the most significant impact. More than a quarter of the day's flights at the airport were grounded as of 5:15 p.m. EST, according to FlightAware.

Those cancellations dealt a blow to operations at Southwest Airlines, the dominant carrier at BWI, which led all U.S. airlines with 126 cancellations Thursday.

Other airports seeing significant cancellation totals on Thanksgiving day includes

Travel disruptions also made a significant impact at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and LaGuardia Airport (LGA), which each had about 10% of the day's flight schedule canceled.

The culprit: the same foul weather that led to the postponement of the nearby Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Midtown Manhattan.

Elsewhere in the Northeast, cancellations created headaches at Washington Reagan National Airport (DCA) and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS).

This week's flight problems came after a chaotic few weeks for air travel in the U.S., which featured a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 — and then tech outages at two of the largest U.S. carriers.

Now, Mother Nature has interfered with holiday travelers' plans.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen had told TPG entering the Thanksgiving rush.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

Major airlines rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions:

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself is typically one of the quietest days of the year at airports.

Forecasters had projected the remnants of the storm could cause lasting delays into Friday, before it peters out by Saturday.

All eyes will be on how Mother Nature cooperates on Saturday and Sunday, as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

Here are some things you should do if you're planning to fly in the next few days.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories (see above) that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

#6018. Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Offers Up To 90,000 Points Back Over Christmas And New Year’s—If You Email The Hotel

Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 World of Hyatt points back per night over Christmas and New Year’s. Christmas Eve and Christmas night run 55,000 points, so you wind up paying net 80,000 points for the two nights after 30,000 points back at a hotel where you can walk out one side to ski school and the other to the village ice rink. It looks open to any member who makes a qualifying booking. Make a new reservation on points November 25 through December 5, 2026 at Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Resort and Spa for a stay December 18, 2026 through January 3, 2027. Book at the full points price. Then email your reservation confirmation to beave-reservations.static@hyatt.com to claim the rebate. You get 15,000 points back per night, up to six nights (90,000 points). Existing reservations don’t qualify so you’d need to re-book. Park Hyatt Beaver Creek points deal by u/David_Copperfield in r/hyatt This amounts to a 27% discount against 55,000 point per night pricing, though this hotel can get even more expensive (e.g. December 22 at 65,000 points). And rooms run around $1,000 per night leading up to Christmas around around $2,000 between Christmas and New Year’s. 40,000 points against peak rates works out nicely. Last Christmas the hotel offered 10,000 points back on a 45,000 point peak night. It was Category 8 then, too, but Hyatt pricing is now much higher at the top end. This year you’re getting 5,000 more points back and still spending 5,000 more for a comparable night. Last year’s deal ended on Christmas Day, while this one covers New Year’s Eve. I’ve never actually stayed here, although I had it booked on points. I caught Covid shortly before the trip, inside the cancellation deadline, and faced a huge cash penalty. I told the hotel that if I had to show up to avoid the charge, I’d sit in the lobby and explain to everyone why the hotel had made it too expensive to avoid exposing them. The hotel’s winter policy is full room rate plus tax if you cancel inside 31 days. Park Hyatt Beaver Creek points deal by u/David_Copperfield in r/hyatt

This amounts to a 27% discount against 55,000 point per night pricing, though this hotel can get even more expensive (e.g. December 22 at 65,000 points). And rooms run around $1,000 per night leading up to Christmas around around $2,000 between Christmas and New Year’s. 40,000 points against peak rates works out nicely.

Last Christmas the hotel offered 10,000 points back on a 45,000 point peak night. It was Category 8 then, too, but Hyatt pricing is now much higher at the top end. This year you’re getting 5,000 more points back and still spending 5,000 more for a comparable night. Last year’s deal ended on Christmas Day, while this one covers New Year’s Eve.

I’ve never actually stayed here, although I had it booked on points. I caught Covid shortly before the trip, inside the cancellation deadline, and faced a huge cash penalty. I told the hotel that if I had to show up to avoid the charge, I’d sit in the lobby and explain to everyone why the hotel had made it too expensive to avoid exposing them. The hotel’s winter policy is full room rate plus tax if you cancel inside 31 days.

#6017. At One Chinese Airport, Passengers Aren’t Allowed To Look Out The Window [Roundup]

News and notes from around the interweb: Somewhat similar to Bucholz Army Airfield on Kwajalein Atoll, Marshall Islands which is a stop on the United Airlines island hopper. Yanji Airport is jointly used by military and civilian aircraft, so passengers are required to close their window shades during takeoff and landing. Because military aircraft have priority, our flight that day was not cleared to land for quite a while, even after the final approach announcement was made. In the end, we spent nearly 30 minutes circling the airport at low altitude with the window shades closed.

#6016. Departing Senate spending kingpins angle for last earmark hurrah

Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

Newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec. 11.

Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.

There's typically some overlap between House and Senate projects that would get weeded out in final negotiations to avoid duplication. But for comparison's sake, House Republicans included nearly 6,700 line items worth $8.2 billion in their earmarked spending bills.

Democrats have signaled they'll push for a continuing resolution into the first quarter of next year enabling them to rewrite the full-year fiscal 2027 bills when they take the gavels in January, possibly upping the overall pot of earmarked funds — or at least divvying up the pie more favorably to blue states and districts.

But that would mean the final attempt by departing lawmakers like Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and longtime Senate GOP leader and senior appropriator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, to deliver for their states might be all for naught.

And top Democrats with substantial earmarking success under GOP governance, such as Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., will have to start from scratch.

Here are some key stats on senators' earmarks in the latest batch of spending bills Collins is trying to get across the finish line.

Naturally, much of the spoils go to Senate Appropriations Committee members, and that's no different this year. But with so many more Democrats requesting projects — often jointly with their fellow delegation member — individual contributions may appear diluted given they have to share the credit.

That dilution shows up in the rankings when allocating credit in a way that avoids double-counting — everyone gets an equal share of his or her joint projects, so $20 million sponsored jointly by two senators will appear as $10 million for each. Solo earmarkers in this scenario face no such dilution.

Using the even-split methodology, the top 10 — all senior appropriators — look like this:

Another way to look at it is by simply adding up every instance of a senator affixing his or her name to a project, which leads to double-counting but gives them full credit for every earmark secured, even with jointly requested projects.

Finally, there's the solo earmarker leaderboard, only counting dollars secured without any co-sponsors:

McConnell and Collins hit the trifecta, ending up among the top three in all three scenarios.

Related: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Unlike the House, where states with the largest populations receive the most funding by virtue of having more representatives securing earmarks, smaller states punch above their weight in the Senate — particularly when their delegations achieve exalted positions of seniority.

Hence Washington state — with Murray and Cantwell, the Commerce Committee ranking member, representing it — is way out in front.

By contrast, the second- and third-most populous states — Texas and Florida — received a grand total of zero earmarked funds, because their GOP senators didn't request any. California, with the largest population, is No. 16 in the ranks; New York is 12th.

Here are the top 10 states by earmarked funds procured in the Senate bills, clearly skewing toward smaller, typically reddish states:

The Transportation-HUD spending bill continues to be the go-to place for earmarks, accounting for 27 percent of all individual projects in the Senate bills and about one-third of all the earmarked dollars. The next-closest bill, Labor-HHS-Education, has half the earmarked amount that the "T-HUD" bill does.

Top agencies and programs with earmarked funds are housed within, that's right, the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, with HUD leading the pack thanks to its ever-popular Community Development Fund accounting for all of that department's earmarks.

Transportation isn't far behind, thanks largely to highway projects, followed by Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration account, which funds community health centers. Defense Department military construction projects and the Army Corps of Engineers round out the group of $1 billion-plus agencies.

Here are the top accounts for earmarked funds in this year's crop of bills:

The biggest individual earmarks are largely within Army Corps accounts funded in the draft Energy-Water bill, with some military construction and transportation projects and two mega NIST-based university construction earmarks thrown in on behalf of Collins and McConnell.

#6015. TSA Demanded United Airlines Suspend A Pilot Over Terror Support, Union Accused Of Resisting, Report Says

TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim. The new report says the intervention happened last week. The pilot hasn’t been named. Neither has the terror group he allegedly supported. Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 update on the reported TSA intervention Wagenheim’s earlier report cited two sources saying United knew of up to six additional crew members who’d expressed support for terrorist groups. United’s pilots union spokesman declined to discuss individual cases. He said the Air Line Pilots Association has a professional standards committee and legal team that assess accusations against its ethics code and United’s workplace guidelines. The Pilot Israel Barred Was Already On Leave In October, Israel prohibited flights with Sina Amjadian serving as crew from arriving in the country. Israeli officials confirmed the restriction after receiving allegations that he’d expressed support for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah. But United said he wasn’t currently flying, having been on leave since 2024. He flew Boeing 737s and wasn’t qualified on long haul aircraft. Apparently there was material showing Iranian leadership imagery and mourning civilians killed in strikes. There are claims of Hezbollah support and that there was a video of him kissing the regime’s emblem. United Pilot Celebrated October 7 Rapes And Murders As ‘Bravery’ I first wrote about Ibrahim Mossallam in November 2023, after his Facebook description of the October 7 attack as “resistance by a brave people.” United removed him from service with pay but he was reported back flying. On October 6, 2026, after the flydubai pilot sought to use his plane as a missile to attack Israel, United told me: We have withheld this pilot from service pending an ongoing review. There were also reports that he returned after just a day, and that two colleagues had given up first class seats to monitor him in the cockpit. United subsequently denied both accounts. A reported claimed the union blocked his firing. TSA Can Order A Pilot Out Of The Cockpit It was striking that the reported order came from TSA. It has authority that extends well beyond passenger checkpoints. Under federal law, a TSA determination that a pilot poses, or is suspected of posing, a terrorism or passenger safety threat requires the Federal Aviation Administration to take action against the pilot’s certificate. TSA can request that the action take effect immediately. It can also issue mandatory security directives to airlines. However, it isn’t clear from the report what legal mechanism is claimed to have been used and doesn’t report an FAA certificate action. It says the pilot’s “TSA credential” was revoked and describes that as Known Crewmember access. TSA can require an airline to remove someone’s access, but losing that privilege doesn’t mean losing a pilot’s license. Flydubai Shows Why The Concern Is Real I don’t need to know a pilot’s politics. But I wouldn’t want someone who celebrates the killing of civilians at the controls of my flight. That calls their judgment into question even without evidence they’ve planned an attack themselves. The September 30 flydubai cockpit attack makes the concern concrete. The co-pilot of that flight planned a suicide attack on the Tel Aviv airport, attacking the captain with an axe to take over the aircraft. He had satisfied the licensing, good conduct and security requirements for the job, and those checks had failed to uncover his extremist intentions. The values of the person in control of an aircraft matter. United Airlines carries cargo consistent with its legal obligations and with U.S. foreign policy. There is no demonstrated connection between that cargo and instances of conflict.

Even the U.N. concluded that the October 7 attacks included rape and gang rape, clear evidence of sexual violence and torture of the hostages. https://apnews.com/article/fe1a35767a63666fe4dc1c97e397177e

Hamas uses civilians as human shields, and hides within the civilian population. They used hospitals as military bases. So while every military conflict includes harm to civilians, frequently at a much greater rate than this one, most of that blame can be assigned to Hamas itself. Whenever you hear about lamentable conditions in Gaza, append “because of Hamas” to the end of that sentence.

Calling Israel’s response to Hamas a genocide strips that term of all meaning. Civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish genocide. The legal question is whether prohibited acts were committed with intent to physically destroy a protected group. Even war crimes do not establish that intent.

Obviously, defeating Hamas and recovering hostages are the obvious alternative explanation for Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Israel targets an armed organization, rather than Palestinians because they are Palestinians (indeed, 21% of Israel’s own population is Arab).

And Israel has taken significant measures in its campaign to protect civilians, which is evidence against an extermination policy. They warn civilians in advance of attacks, and evacuate civilian populations. The argument doesn’t even depend on those efforts being ultimately effective to count against a claim of genocide, which is a claim about intent.

There are statements from some terrible people in Israel’s government that are pretty inflammatory (there are some terrible people in our government, or who run for office, who say inflammatory things as well). Those statements do not express operative government policy. Critics often cite National Security Minister Ben Gvir, but most Americans think that’s a military position. It’s not. It’s like head of the police, but he’s been given a more grandiose-sounding title.

The International Court of Justice has held that genocidal intent must be the only reasonable inference from the pattern of conduct. Evidence compatible with other purposes defeats that inference. https://www.icj-cij.org/node/103223

So no, there is not a genocide in Gaza you ignorant fool.

@Gary – a valiant attempt to speak rationally to the irrational though….In the end, people will believe what they believe and a lot of people believe in all kinds of nonsense. It’s futile. Actions and good deeds are far more important.

Happy Thanksgiving to you and your family!

#6014. For ‘Denuclearization,’ Trump Should Build Up to Build Down

The president ought to take a page from Reagan’s Cold War playbook.

The U.S. Navy Ohio-class ballistic missile submarine USS Tennessee returns to Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay, Ga., in 2013.

Mass Communication Specialist First Class James Kimber/U.S. Navy/Handout via Reuters

President Trump left his Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin last week still dreaming of a denuclearization agreement with his great-power counterparts. But Trump’s long-held ambition to achieve the deep reductions in nuclear weaponry that Ronald Reagan secured with his Soviet counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s clashes with reality. Chinese and Russian officials may now be speaking the language of “strategic stability,” but Trump would be wise to recognize that these pronouncements are intended to deter him from taking the steps necessary to strengthen America’s nuclear deterrence.

Unlike Gorbachev in the final years of the Cold War, neither Xi nor Putin currently has any appetite for meaningful arms-control negotiations. Xi acts as if his geopolitical position compares favorably with America’s. Both men are wielding their nuclear power to weaken America’s security and dissolve its alliances. Consider Putin’s nuclear threats during the war in Ukraine and Xi’s campaign of coercion in the western Pacific, which is shielded by China’s growing nuclear arsenal.

Kyle Balzer is a resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute where he specializes in nuclear strategy and policy.

On “For ‘Denuclearization,’ Trump Should Build Up to Build Down”

Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

First, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you plan to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

We’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

Another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

#6011. Warning For Families Traveling To California: New Booster Seat Law Covers Kids Through Age 15

I have a California trip coming up with my family. If I hadn’t seen this on Twitter, it wouldn’t have occurred to me that my 8-year-old daughter might need a booster for the ride from the airport. We live in Texas, where she’s aged out of the child seat requirement. Starting January 1, 2027, California will insist on measuring how the belt fits her in the car we actually wind up with from National, Avis or Uber. She could fit the belt in our car at home and need a booster in the SUV we get assigned to, but she’s already aged out of the California law that requires the rental company to have a child seat for her. We might have to bring one with us just in case. New Booster Seat Rules Go Into Effect January 1 Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 435 in October 2025. Through the end of this year, a child 8 or older isn’t required to use a car seat or booster seat. Starting January 1, 2027 the rule becomes that a 15 year old requires a booster seat unless all five of these conditions are met: Their back is all the way against the vehicle seat. Their knees bend over the front edge of the cushion. The shoulder belt sits snugly across the middle of their chest and shoulder, clear of their neck. The lap belt sits as low as it can, touching their thighs. They can keep that position for the whole ride. An 8-year old who meets this can ride with just a belt, while a 15-year old who fails to meet one of these conditions needs a booster. Here’s a demonstration of the fit test: . What Happens At The Rental Counter And The Uber Pickup California’s rental car law requires agencies to have a compliant seat available for rent on request for children under 8. This new law doesn’t change that. I don’t count on rental companies having a car seat for my young son, even where it’s required and I’ve reserved it. If they’re out of seats, or the buckle’s broken in the one they have, my wife or I has to wait at the airport while the other one goes to Target. I wrote about a mother at the Atlanta airport who said the seats Avis rented her for her babies didn’t work. Avis says airport availability can be limited. At participating Hertz locations, the AAA rate includes a child seat with an advance reservation, subject to availability. ‘Availability’ is doing a lot of work here. Meanwhile, this also has a huge effect on rideshare (and taxis). They’re not required to have a booster. And if I don’t have one, I’m responsible for violations and the driver can decline the ride without it. Los Angeles and San Francisco do have Uber Car Seat. You reserve it in advance, pay a $10 surcharge and get one. It tops out at 49 inches and 65 pounds. A 50-inch child is too tall for the seat Uber supplies and can still need a booster for that ride. And a family with two kids who need restraints still has to supply the second one (or split up and take two Ubers). California is extreme here, although there are various outlier rules already. The U.K. requires boosters until age 12 or 135 centimeters while Germany is age 12 or 150 centimeters. Is This Really A Safety Issue? When a kid scoots forward because their knees don’t bend over a deep seat, the lap belt can ride up over their belly. The theory of the booster seat is that it helps put the force of a crash on the bones of the pelvis. In a study of 388 children and five vehicles, at least 90% of kids 4 feet 9 or taller fit the belt in the compact car and small SUV. Only 77% fit in the large SUV. A study of Washington state crash records found that over a 13 year period looking at 8-12 year olds, 11% in boosters were injured while 15% were injured wearing belts alone. Researchers calculated a 19% reduction in injury risk with a booster, while 0.3% in each group had an incapacitating injury. The study couldn’t establish a difference between booster and no booster for those serious outcomes. There’s a claim of a 45% reduction in injury risk but that’s from a study of 4- to 8-year olds, and even there it seems there’s no statistically significant reduction in injuries. Probably the best we can say is that there’s a real benefit in crash fatality rates for young children but there’s no data suggesting any benefit for 13- to 15-year-olds, and there’s not even any estimate for California preventing injuries with this new law. Who Wanted This Law? Would it surprise you to learn that this bill was supported by the Juvenile Products Manufacturers Association, which is a lobby group for companies that sell booser seats? I’m not sure how a police officer at a traffic stop is supposed to judge whether a child can hold the belt fit position throughout the entire ride. The base fine for violations is $100 the first time and $250 thereafter plus assessments. And 60% of the fines collected go to local health departments to help buy more booster seats. In Car Seats as Contraception, researchers estimate that women with two children still covered by their state’s car seat mandate were 0.73 percentage points less likely to have a third child that year. Fitting three seats across can mean buying a new car. The study couldn’t establish a difference between booster and no booster for those serious outcomes.

There’s a claim of a 45% reduction in injury risk but that’s from a study of 4- to 8-year olds, and even there it seems there’s no statistically significant reduction in injuries. Probably the best we can say is that there’s a real benefit in crash fatality rates for young children but there’s no data suggesting any benefit for 13- to 15-year-olds, and there’s not even any estimate for California preventing injuries with this new law.

Would it surprise you to learn that this bill was supported by the Juvenile Products Manufacturers Association, which is a lobby group for companies that sell booser seats? I’m not sure how a police officer at a traffic stop is supposed to judge whether a child can hold the belt fit position throughout the entire ride. The base fine for violations is $100 the first time and $250 thereafter plus assessments. And 60% of the fines collected go to local health departments to help buy more booster seats. In Car Seats as Contraception, researchers estimate that women with two children still covered by their state’s car seat mandate were 0.73 percentage points less likely to have a third child that year. Fitting three seats across can mean buying a new car. Typical nonsensical California overregulation. A true nanny state we have here.

Now there’s going to be a teen tourism lobby, e.g. theme parks, in California.

Nonsensical? It really is a safety issue. If a child does not fit the seat properly, they can be seriously injured. It is based on evidence-based recommendations and bioengineering recommendations. There is literature from Washington State (see below) showing a 19% reduction in overall injury rates, and another study showing a 10% absolute reduction in serious injury when boosters are used. Studies on this question are somewhat limited because the research is technically challenging, but what we do have supports a significant benefit.

Car manufacturers state that a child must be able to sit with their knees bent over the front of the seat, their back firmly against the backrest, and the seatbelt across the chest, not the neck. If they can’t, they need a booster. Plenty of kids who are 8 years old are too short or small to be safely restrained by the car’s restraint system, and a booster improves their chances of making it through a collision without serious injury. My own daughter (I live in Texas) was in a booster until she was nearly 12 because of her height.

Other states have similar, albeit with some variation, laws: Colorado, Washington, Louisiana and Minnesota. This law simply ensures people use their cars safely.

While many laws, regardless of jurisdiction, are silly, this one is based on best practices to improve children’s safety.

So, overall, while I know this is inconvenient, it is far from an overreach by a “nanny state.” A big failing of this law, it seems, is that rental car agencies are not required to support their customer’s compliance by providing a booster for older children.

Reading these seating requirements, I realized that I — a petite 5′ 2″ senior citizen — would have ALWAYS required a booster seat because all seat belts rub against my neck when they are worn correctly. I jerryrig seatbelt positions so they do not chafe against my neck. I would imagine everyone who is smaller shares a similar experience.

I think Kevin works for OSHA. Long winded tripe.

California is run by special interests, and sometimes grifters, who want more money in their pockets at the expense of the rest of us. Affordability be dammed, especially while they can still blame Trump.

This is feel good legislation with very little, really zero, science behind it. This from the party of “believe the science”. This is clearly, like a lot of legislation, driven by the lobbyists for the car seat manufacturers.

I don’t know what a car seat costs, but I’m going to risk the ticket if I’m visiting California, vs buying on there, and I’m going to leave the kid with the wife outside the car rental office. Or, in most places I rent anymore, I just go get the car without going in the office.

It’s OK though, in California they have big signs at the rental car agency telling you that renting a car causes cancer. And, I’m serious.

Is there any issue too small for the government not to override our own cost-benefit analysis?

Have you heard about California’s mandate for tires with lower rolling resistance, even though they give you less grip? I prefer better accident avoidance to better gas mileage. Give us the facts and let us make the choice!

15. The age at which one can apply for a learner’s permit in Kalifornia.

“I think Kevin works for OSHA. Long winded tripe.”

Or that Juvenile Products Manufacturers Association.

All your statistics measure age and not height/weight. The point of the regulation is that height/weight are the actually appropriate measurements rather than a rough approximation from age. Most kids aren’t outliers, so the 15 year old won’t be in a booster unless they’re extremely small.

It’s the same reason car seats for babies and toddlers show weights and heights instead of ages for each style and facing of the car seat.

This is a ridiculous law that none of us in CA asked for. My daughter is extremely petite. She’s in her 20s now, but when she was 15 she was still 4’11” – I would have had to keep her in a booster seat halfway through high school. Absurd. I’m 5’5″ and find that in many cars even if I adjust the seatbelt it goes over my throat, not the middle of my chest.

Add in the new ridiculous tire requirements too – that have less grip – last week I had to drive 80 miles each way to an appointment in the rain. I made sure to grab new tires the week before (needed them anyway), before this kicks in too.

And they wonder why there’s a bit of a mass exodus from CA…

Anyone reading this born before 1972? Congratulations you survived childhood without a seat belt.

Sure and have the state doesn’t have insurance. Useless nanny state

Worth knowing for Disneyland and San Diego trips. Rental counters only have to stock seats for under 8s, so for older kids a backless booster from home is the safe bet. They’re light and fit in a carry-on

No self respecting teen is going to use a booster seat when they are in middle school.

this law is going to be DOA in terms of adherence.

Sadly there’s no lack of insipid comments that don’t address the problem.

A reasonable adjustment to the law might be something like requiring this for residents in their own vehicles and giving more leeway to taxis and rideshares to allow for judgement calls for borderline situations.

@Christian, exactly. that would be a reasonable solution, though I would extend the flexibility to visitors getting rental cars. And if the residents do not like it, they have the ability to vote out those who made the law (unlike visitors to the state)

#6009. Chris Van Hollen’s Anti-Israel Turn

The Maryland senator has become an unlikely opponent of the Jewish state — and that’s boosted his fortunes in the Democratic Party.

Senator Chris Van Hollen (D., Md.) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C, November 19, 2026.

It’s a well-established gambit. A politician starts criticizing Jews. He gains followers. His attacks grow, along with his political power.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen (D.), who is challenging Chuck Schumer for the position of Senate majority leader, is adopting this playbook. Van Hollen, who alleged in a recent New York Times op-ed that Israelis have “increasingly undermined American interests and values,” has become one of the foremost critics of the Jewish state in Congress. Backed by progressives such as Bernie Sanders, he is basking in his newfound fame. His foray into the Senate leadership contest coincided with his push to strip provisions concerning U.S. security cooperation with Israel from the National Defense Authorization Act. These and other broadsides have made him a darling of the anti-Zionist left. Regardless of whether he supplants Schumer, Van Hollen is pushing the Senate ever leftward on its policy toward Israel.

Senator Chris Van Hollen (D., Md.) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C, November 19, 2026.

Daniel J. Samet is a Jeane Kirkpatrick Fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. He interned for then-Representative Van Hollen in 2015.

#6008. 82% Of Americans Fly Once A Year Or Less—And Don’t Know The Rules

Last Thanksgiving, if you saw an open aisle seat on Southwest Airlines, you were welcome to take it. Do exactly what you learned a year ago and this Thanksgiving you’re the guy holding up the aisle because the passenger behind you has a boarding pass for your seat, and you’re getting scolded by a flight attendant. Travel rules change! Boarding at Southwest has changed! You might not even know you’re going to have to pay baggage fees if you don’t travel every year. every behavior you see in the airport makes perfect sense when you remember >50% of Americans fly less than once a year— Alexis (@aleozimok) November 25, 2026 The actual number is higher than this. In YouGov’s November 17–19 poll of 1,092 U.S. adult citizens, 34% said they fly less than once a year, 32% said never and 16% said once a year. That’s 66% who fly less than annually (including never) and 82% who fly once a year or less. Just 34% said they’d flown in the past 12 months and 65% said they hadn’t. Who’s Actually In The Seat Next To You? In 2015, then-American Airlines president Scott Kirby said 87% of American’s customers flew them just once in the previous year and generated about half their revenue. Kirby was explaining why American needed basic economy. For every 100 American adults who flew in 2017, 24 took just one trip, and all 100 averaged 5.3 trips apiece. In the 1970s and 1980s, roughly half the air trips Americans took were for business. Personal trips already accounted for about 70% before the pandemic and 74% in 2025. My line when business travel dried up during the pandemic was that “all airline passengers are Spirit Airlines passengers now.” Mask rules drove most of the reported trouble. Of 5,981 unruly passenger reports the Federal Aviation Administration received in 2021, 4,290 involved masks. But losing the regulars sprinkled through coach mattered too. What It Costs To Go See Family In 1977, before deregulation, 25% of U.S. adults flew that year and 63% had ever flown. I’ve written about how much less work it takes to buy a ticket. Between 1995 and 2025, the average domestic fare fell from $618 to $387 in 2025 dollars, a 37% drop excluding bag and seat fees. Fee-inclusive costs are down, too. In a separate YouGov poll earlier in November, 18% of people with family incomes under $50,000 had flown in the past year, compared with 66% at $100,000 or more. Family travel multiplies the cost of tickets across each person while driving costs are constant. AAA expects 72.9 million Americans to drive this Thanksgiving holiday and just under 6 million to fly domestically. Frequent Flyers Share The Same Frustrations With Once A Year Travelers YouGov also asked which things are a major problem with U.S. air travel. Price topped these everyday complaints for both groups. Called this a major problem   Fly less than annually(excludes “never”)   Fly at least annually High fares 64% 66% Delays and cancellations 42% 50% Extra or hidden fees 42% 49% Long security lines 35% 36% But The Travel Experience Is Very Different My status gets me on early enough to find space for my bag. When a flight cancels, I’m looking up alternatives on my phone while I’m in line for an agent. I still have days when I wonder how anybody who does this once a year manages to get where they’re going. A parent buys four tickets and gets a seat map full of prices. Will their eight-year-old sit next to a stranger if they don’t pay? American tells families on one reservation who can’t get seats together that they’re better off skipping seats for everybody than selecting the two they can see. The person who took their laptop out at security on the way there and left it in the bag on the way home may have followed instructions both times. It depends on the scanner in their lane. Say you book a 40 minute connection. You don’t know whether that’s a good idea or not, and may not even know or understand the connecting time, just the departure and arrival times. The airline ends boarding 15 minutes before departure. You’ve got 25 minutes even if you’re on time, some of which you’ll spend getting off the first plane. And if your regional jet on the first segment valet tags your bag, you’re waiting for it on the jet bridge, too. I wound up on Southwest’s first day of assigned seating because American went through three itineraries trying to get me to Washington and I finally bought a ticket to Baltimore. At the gate, Southwest called Group 3 to line up under a sign that still said Group 1. Where, exactly, was the passenger who stopped to read the sign supposed to stand? I’m home this Thanksgiving. I traveled the week before and will travel again the week after. I like to avoid ‘amateur day’. And when I do travel I try to go where other people aren’t. My favorite Thanksgiving trip was Chennai (I wanted to have Thanksgiving dinner with Indians), and I had to explain to CBP on arrival back in the states that we’d done that because it was cheaper booking Lufthansa first class (on points) than going to visit my wife’s family. And if your regional jet on the first segment valet tags your bag, you’re waiting for it on the jet bridge, too.

I wound up on Southwest’s first day of assigned seating because American went through three itineraries trying to get me to Washington and I finally bought a ticket to Baltimore. At the gate, Southwest called Group 3 to line up under a sign that still said Group 1. Where, exactly, was the passenger who stopped to read the sign supposed to stand?

I’m home this Thanksgiving. I traveled the week before and will travel again the week after. I like to avoid ‘amateur day’. And when I do travel I try to go where other people aren’t. My favorite Thanksgiving trip was Chennai (I wanted to have Thanksgiving dinner with Indians), and I had to explain to CBP on arrival back in the states that we’d done that because it was cheaper booking Lufthansa first class (on points) than going to visit my wife’s family.

Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. More About Gary »

What’s amazing to me is how many people don’t realize they can cancel or change their flight without having to pay a “penalty”. (Assuming they’re not in Basic)

Unless you fly out of HSV where 70% of all airline passengers are weekly business travelers.

I cannot understand why I have to remove my belt, even as a Trusted Traveler, while keeping my watch that contains 10x the metal.

That shows that frequent flyers are fat cats that must be punished! Make them pay their fair share!

Punish them with high taxes on rental cars and hotels. Frequent flyer miles are an even worse sign if their greed and need to be punished and taxed. The basic, occasional flyer should get the most miles, not the rich guy that already has lots of miles. Tax the rich. Tax those miles, like 50% (50% of your annual miles taken by the IRS and given to the poor, then a wealth tax on your balance). AOC must be President in 2028. Pay your fair share.

@KIRK: “I cannot understand why I have to remove my belt, even as a Trusted Traveler, while keeping my watch that contains 10x the metal.”

Kirk, I realized almost two years ago that my belt is best kept on, while I remove my watch, and stuff it with container containing the carry-ons. First of all, it takes less time to put on my watch than my belt. Second, I have yet to confront a screening station in major European airports that catch my belt. OK, the trick is don’t try it with a Texas style belt buckle. I have a web belt, with link that is small amount of metal. Oh, and I never try to go through a European screening station that makes me show my belt is off before going through.

I used to fly alot for business. I dread even getting on planes now.

Between the extra fees for just about everything, FAs for the most part hating their jobs, people dressed liked their headed for the bedroom and not a trip, planes leave and arrive late, FF miles pretty much worth nothing, CEOs complaining they need to add more premium seats to gouge their customers more, its no wonder why people do not fly, I pretty much drive if under 750 miles, for the 12h of driving half that time would be spent getting to the airport, waiting for flight, delays, then if lucky landing on time, costing 5x what it costs to drive to the same location and much less hassle.

Until the customers decide they are not going to put up with these issues they will continue.

Airlines could absolutely care less, they are more concerned pushing their CC ads than operating a airline.

People are oblivious and stupid. Simple as that

Surprised OPM flying is still that much of a percentage. Good to see it going down every year.

We have flown quite a bit (vacations) and want to feel as safe as possible. So, whatever the airlines want to do is fine with me.

We avoid busy times (lThanksgiving, Christmas, New Year’s, etc.). Unless we can fly out a week before the holiday and return a week or so after it, we would not fly during those times.

In general, we avoid international flights from late April – mid-October. The airports major cities around the world can be packed. We do not fly U.S.-based airlines. With the many articles this great site has posted, we agree with every less than positive things that they have shared. There are some great airlines out (that care about their passengers) there, but sadly. we prefer not to fly American, Delta or United. We will do an occasional short flight on Alaska.

This all reminds me of the comedy at Christmas Mass in 1970…

Basically, there was a BIG overhaul in 1970. The regulars knew the new process, but your Christmas/Easter attendees…didn’t. So you had e.g. half of the congregation kneeling at the wrong time.

The right travel credit card is important for any trip, as it can earn points or miles and provide valuable travel protections. But when you travel for months at a time, other factors — including no foreign transaction fees, international acceptance and benefits you can use outside the U.S. — become especially important.

Living and working on the road without a permanent home base puts these priorities to the test. The best card benefits solve practical problems and remain useful long after a typical vacation would have ended.

With that in mind, these are some of the best cards for long-term travelers and digital nomads.

Now, let's dive into what each of these cards has to offer.

All of the welcome bonus valuations in this guide are based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

The is best for long-term travelers who want broad travel protections, premium lounge access and flexible points in one card.

Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve is an excellent card for long-term travelers because it earns at least 4 points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining purchases.

The card's up-to-$300 annual travel credit is straightforward to use, while Chase Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access can provide a place to work, eat and recharge between flights. The card also charges no foreign transaction fees.

Its travel protections are another reason why it's a great choice for digital nomads. Baggage delay coverage, for example, can help cover essentials when your checked bag doesn't arrive on time. Trip delay and trip cancellation/interruption coverage can also soften the financial hit when plans unravel.

Plus, Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to hotel and airline partners, including fan favorites like United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt.

However, the card carries a $795 annual fee, and several of its statement credits are tied to particular merchants.

Cardholders can get up to $500 in statement credits each calendar year for qualifying prepaid stays of at least two nights through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, with a maximum of $250 per transaction. It can be a fantastic perk when a long trip calls for a comfortable hotel reset between apartment stays or after a long-haul flight.

If you spend most of the year outside the U.S., weigh the $795 annual fee against the benefits you’ll use regularly.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The is best for digital nomads who can use its extensive lounge network, hotel elite status and premium perks.

Welcome bonus: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards Points after spending $12,000 on purchases within the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The Amex Platinum comes offers one of the largest airport lounge networks available. The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes access to Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required for Priority Pass Select).

That pairs nicely with a high earning rate on flights booked directly with the airline as well as up to a $200 airline fee statement credit every calendar year on your selected qualifying airline (enrollment required; terms apply).

Cardmembers can transfer their Membership Rewards points to Amex's airline and hotel partners, opening up award flights and hotel stays worldwide.

Several other card benefits lend themselves nicely to travelers who stay in hotels, rather than long-term rentals. Hotel elite status, including Hilton Honors Gold Elite, Leaders Club Sterling and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite, can make your stays more comfortable (enrollment required).

The up-to-$600 annual lodging statement credit adds more value to the card and can give you an excuse to add luxe stays to your itinerary. It is split into two up to $300 semiannual credits and applies to qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe, Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®. (Airbnb Luxe and THC require a minimum two-night stay; FHR will also require a minimum two-night stay beginning Jan. 1, 2027; terms apply).

It's worth noting that you likely won't be able to use every statement credit. Someone spending a lot of time outside the U.S. may have trouble using several U.S.-focused perks, including Uber Cash (for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders) and Walmart+.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

The Venture X is best for digital nomads who want premium travel perks and simple rewards on everyday spending.

Welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

For digital nomads, the Venture X works well because of how little strategy it requires, at home or abroad. It earns 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases outside bonus categories. These flat-rate, hassle-free rewards are useful when your spending habits change from one country to the next.

The card allows you to transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel partners. That's even more flexibility when your travels take you all over the world.

The card's $300 annual Capital One travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles (worth $100 toward bookings made through the Capital One Travel portal) are very easy ways to offset the annual fee.

Primary cardholders also receive complimentary access to Capital One Lounges, Capital One Landings and participating Priority Pass lounges.

The card offers cellphone protection when you pay your monthly wireless bill with it (up to $800 per eligible claim, with a $50 deductible and a maximum of two claims per 12-month period). That's useful when your phone is your boarding pass, map and connection to work.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The offers a useful middle ground for digital nomads who want strong everyday rewards without paying a hefty annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months.

At $95 a year, the Strata Premier is the easiest card on this list to justify. Its protections are particularly practical when you live out of a suitcase. The card's 24-month extended warranty can be especially useful when living on the road, as nomadic life can take a toll on electronics and other gear.

Cardholders can transfer ThankYou points to more than 20 airline and hotel partners. There's also an annual $100 hotel benefit per calendar year for a single hotel stay (of $500 or more; excluding taxes and fees) booked through CitiTravel.com or by calling Citi. That's a fast way to offset the card's $95 annual fee.

The Strata Premier offers fewer statement credits than pricier cards. Its $95 annual fee makes it a good fit if you’re traveling on a budget or want an affordable second card.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Premier.

The is best for everyday spending abroad, thanks to its earning rate on eligible foreign transactions.

Welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

For digital nomads, the card's value comes from a benefit that applies well beyond Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights. Cardholders earn 3 Atmos Rewards points per dollar spent on foreign transactions, whether that's a hotel stay, meal, pharmacy visit or souvenir.

You'll also get a 10% rewards bonus on points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account.

Atmos Rewards points can be redeemed for flights on Oneworld carriers and other airline partners, in addition to Alaska and Hawaiian.

The annual Global Companion Award provides a 25,000-point discount when two travelers book award travel on the same itinerary. Based on our valuations, this benefit alone is worth $400. That's enough to justify the annual fee, even if you never touch the other Alaska or Hawaiian-specific benefits.

Cardholders who spend $60,000 in a card anniversary year can earn an additional Global Companion Award worth up to 100,000 points. Since these awards can be used in any class of service, the larger award could be particularly valuable for a premium-cabin or long-haul partner redemption.

That same $60,000 in spending earns 30,000 status points. Combined with the 10,000 status points awarded after each account anniversary, you'd have enough for Atmos Gold status (mapped to Oneworld Sapphire). On eligible itineraries, that's good for business-class lounge access — even when you're flying economy — priority check-in and boarding, preferred seating and extra baggage.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Summit card.

Many long-term travelers and digital nomads run businesses from the road. These travelers may find it useful to have one or more business cards as well.

One business card that's particularly well-suited to this lifestyle is the (see rates and fees).

This card earns 3 points per dollar spent on travel, shipping, social media and search engine advertising, and cable, internet and phone services (on the first $150,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The Ink Business Preferred also offers cellphone insurance, primary rental car insurance on business-related rentals and no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

When you live out of a suitcase, the best card benefits aren't always flashy. What matters is what follows you: protections when your laptop dies or your flight gets canceled, solid rewards on everyday spending in any currency and lounges in the airports you actually pass through.

A long list of statement credits might only be great if you'll be back home in a few days. For extended travel, it's more important to pick the card that works wherever you wake up tomorrow.
