#6005. Why Austin’s Airport Is Packed While Others Feel Empty—It’s Not Just About Number Of Gates

Austin’s airport can be so crowded that you can barely move through the terminal. Passengers spill out of gate areas into the corridor, where everyone else is trying to get somewhere. Then you visit another airport, walk through an almost empty concourse, and wonder why we’re spending billions building more gates there. Adam Nathan put together an interesting comparison of passengers per airport gate. Austin comes out at 637,000, Seattle at 592,000, and Washington Dulles at just 212,000. There’s a lot to learn from this, but the gates aren’t interchangeable, and neither are the conclusions you can draw from them. For instance, Nathan flags that Austin reduced its gates this year. That’s true – it closed its South Terminal with three gates – but those gates handled just 3.6% of the airport’s passengers last year. And Charlotte’s large number of regional jet gates makes average passengers per gate look much more reasonable – when outside of that E concourse, the place is a dense mess. Adam Nathan’s airport passengers-per-gate comparison Austin Closed Gates, But They Were Largely Immaterial Nathan’s slide specifically refers to the South Terminal closure, and that’s fair. Austin closed the separate Allegiant and Frontier facility on March 31, moving those airlines into the main terminal April 1. The site is needed for new taxiways and the airport’s construction program to grow. However, the airport’s 2025 passenger totals show how lightly those three gates were compared with the main terminal: 2025 traffic South Terminal Main terminal Passengers 771,354 20,895,498 Share of airport passengers 3.6% 96.4% Gates 3 gates 34 gates Annual passengers per gate 257,118 614,573 Frontier carried 553,311 passengers and Allegiant 218,043. Each South Terminal gate handled about 42% as many passengers as a main terminal gate. Moving those flights into an already crowded building wasn’t ideal, but losing three of 37 nominal gates didn’t mean losing 8% of the airport’s passenger capacity. There are actually three different construction stories here: The South Terminal’s three boarding positions went away to make room for work on the airfield. The three new gates at the west end of the main terminal were built to offset gates being taken out for expansion, including the underground connection to the new concourse. Austin is building Concourse M, a separate six-gate facility reached by bus, in addition to the new 26-gate Concourse B. Those six gates will help maintain operations during construction. West Gate Expansion So commenters suggesting “reopen the closed gates” aren’t familiar with the airport. This is space being used to build out the airport. Terminal width matters, too. Boarding lines, arriving passengers and people walking to other gates all compete for the same floor space. Austin’s master plan identified 89,600 square feet of circulation corridors after the 2019 east expansion, compared with a modeled requirement of 125,350 square feet at 16 million annual passengers and 173,650 at 22 million (almost twice the space). Atlanta’s Concourse D project is a good contrast because it widens the building from 60 feet to 99 feet, increases the depth of gate waiting areas from 20 feet to 35 feet, and reduces the gate count from 40 to 34, with all remaining gates accommodating larger aircraft. Hold passenger traffic constant and passengers per gate rises nearly 18% simply because the denominator shrank—even as passengers get more space. An airport can have fewer gates, higher passengers per gate, and a substantially less density for a better experience walking through the terminal. Charlotte Shows Why A Low Passenger Count Doesn’t Mean An Idle Gate Charlotte comes out at about 432,000 passengers per gate, well below Austin. If you’ve tried to get through its piers during a connecting bank, that doesn’t describe the experience very well. The airport has an enormous regional operation. It has 45 gates on Concourse E and that concourse handles more aircraft operations per gate than the others. A gate turning regional jets all day can move fewer passengers than a gate with fewer departures on larger aircraft. Charlotte’s planned expansion adds gates and improves aircraft circulation without widening the existing B and C corridors. The ends of the piers at Washington National has the same problem. Why Bigger Planes Don’t Produce The Highest Numbers Flights per gate is a more direct starting point for judging how hard an airline is using its gates. But passengers per gate adds size of aircraft, carrying more people without adding departures. So the surprising part of this comparison is how dense airports with relatively little widebody flying are. But narrowbody gates tend to turn over more frequently. Long haul aircraft often need longer turns, and their schedules are constrained by overnight flying, arrival times and connections at the other end. An international gate can sit empty for hours. And you can’t just replace every regional jet with an Airbus A321. Some routes can’t support it, some passengers value frequency, and some gates and alleyways can’t accommodate it. Upgauging also puts more people into the waiting area for each departure. Dulles Already Has Room To Grow? Washington Dulles is the most provocative comparison because it looks so lightly used while pursuing a roughly $20 billion reconstruction program. I’ve criticized the economics of that plan. First, the slide labels Dulles as having 137 jetbridge gates, excluding 16 remote stands. The airport authority’s 2025 bond documents tell a different story: 121 aircraft parking positions, including regional hardstands without boarding bridges, and excluding 16 remote hardstands. Adding those remote positions produces 137. Since that inventory Concourse E opening November 10 with 14 new gates. Its flexible layout can accommodate a large widebody in space used by two smaller narrowbodies. The number of usable gates actually depends on which planes park there. The same bond documents show 7.3 scheduled departures per gate per day at National versus 3.4 at Dulles for June 2025. The question is how much of that unused time airlines can profitably use. A quiet international concourse at one hour doesn’t establish spare gates where United needs them at another. Nor does it address the 1980s temporary midfield C/D concourse. Replacing outdated buildings, improving train access and getting passengers out of mobile lounges can be worthwhile even without a shortage of gates, although the proposed cost of the project would drive up expenses so much that Dulles could never support a low cost carrier flight again. Analyzing Additional Airports Seattle is working its gates hard. The Port of Seattle’s master plan includes a second terminal with 19 additional gates. Dallas Love Field Is Noticeably Absent This analysis set a threshold of airports with at least 25 gates, so a 20-gate airport serving around 17 million passengers per year gets excluded. That’s roughly 850,000 passengers per gate. Austin leads this sample, not the country. Congress agreed to remove and legally cap gates at the airport as a way of entrenching incumbent positions of American Airlines (limiting competition to their DFW operation) and Southwest (limiting the ability to compete at Love Field) – gates were actually destroyed, in fact six became a Lincoln dealership. Former hubs naturally have leftover capacity. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh were built to handle connecting operations that shrank. Pittsburgh has a reduced 53-gate footprint, rather than its old 75-gate layout. Detroit is lighter use than Atlanta, but that doesn’t mean flights can be re-routed to a different hub. Local demand, fares, geography and the connections already available determine whether shifting a flight makes more or less money. Similarly, San Antonio isn’t interchangeable with Austin, Ontario with Los Angeles, or San Jose with San Francisco. It’s Time To Build—But Users Have To Pay Gates are only one constraint. Runways, weather and available airspace determine how many planes can arrive and depart. Nearby airports may need the same airspace. Taxiway bottlenecks can keep a landed plane from reaching an empty gate. Security, baggage systems, customs and curbs can each run out of capacity too. Austin needs more room for people. Charlotte needs people and airplanes to move through the airport better, wider concourses (and higher ceilings!). Dulles needs to… not do the thing that was announced. And none of this explains why growing airports with millions of customers should get taxpayer money. Airports can issue revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid. I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens. Charlotte’s planned expansion adds gates and improves aircraft circulation without widening the existing B and C corridors. The ends of the piers at Washington National has the same problem. Why Bigger Planes Don’t Produce The Highest Numbers Flights per gate is a more direct starting point for judging how hard an airline is using its gates. But passengers per gate adds size of aircraft, carrying more people without adding departures. So the surprising part of this comparison is how dense airports with relatively little widebody flying are. But narrowbody gates tend to turn over more frequently. Long haul aircraft often need longer turns, and their schedules are constrained by overnight flying, arrival times and connections at the other end. An international gate can sit empty for hours. And you can’t just replace every regional jet with an Airbus A321. Some routes can’t support it, some passengers value frequency, and some gates and alleyways can’t accommodate it. Upgauging also puts more people into the waiting area for each departure. Dulles Already Has Room To Grow? Washington Dulles is the most provocative comparison because it looks so lightly used while pursuing a roughly $20 billion reconstruction program. I’ve criticized the economics of that plan. First, the slide labels Dulles as having 137 jetbridge gates, excluding 16 remote stands. The airport authority’s 2025 bond documents tell a different story: 121 aircraft parking positions, including regional hardstands without boarding bridges, and excluding 16 remote hardstands. Adding those remote positions produces 137. Since that inventory Concourse E opening November 10 with 14 new gates. Its flexible layout can accommodate a large widebody in space used by two smaller narrowbodies. The number of usable gates actually depends on which planes park there. The same bond documents show 7.3 scheduled departures per gate per day at National versus 3.4 at Dulles for June 2025. The question is how much of that unused time airlines can profitably use. A quiet international concourse at one hour doesn’t establish spare gates where United needs them at another. Nor does it address the 1980s temporary midfield C/D concourse. Replacing outdated buildings, improving train access and getting passengers out of mobile lounges can be worthwhile even without a shortage of gates, although the proposed cost of the project would drive up expenses so much that Dulles could never support a low cost carrier flight again. Analyzing Additional Airports Seattle is working its gates hard. The Port of Seattle’s master plan includes a second terminal with 19 additional gates. Dallas Love Field Is Noticeably Absent This analysis set a threshold of airports with at least 25 gates, so a 20-gate airport serving around 17 million passengers per year gets excluded. That’s roughly 850,000 passengers per gate. Austin leads this sample, not the country. Congress agreed to remove and legally cap gates at the airport as a way of entrenching incumbent positions of American Airlines (limiting competition to their DFW operation) and Southwest (limiting the ability to compete at Love Field) – gates were actually destroyed, in fact six became a Lincoln dealership. Former hubs naturally have leftover capacity. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh were built to handle connecting operations that shrank. Pittsburgh has a reduced 53-gate footprint, rather than its old 75-gate layout. Detroit is lighter use than Atlanta, but that doesn’t mean flights can be re-routed to a different hub. Local demand, fares, geography and the connections already available determine whether shifting a flight makes more or less money. Similarly, San Antonio isn’t interchangeable with Austin, Ontario with Los Angeles, or San Jose with San Francisco. It’s Time To Build—But Users Have To Pay Gates are only one constraint. Runways, weather and available airspace determine how many planes can arrive and depart. Nearby airports may need the same airspace. Taxiway bottlenecks can keep a landed plane from reaching an empty gate. Security, baggage systems, customs and curbs can each run out of capacity too. Austin needs more room for people. Charlotte needs people and airplanes to move through the airport better, wider concourses (and higher ceilings!). Dulles needs to… not do the thing that was announced. And none of this explains why growing airports with millions of customers should get taxpayer money. Airports can issue revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid. I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens. Nathan’s slide specifically refers to the South Terminal closure, and that’s fair. Austin closed the separate Allegiant and Frontier facility on March 31, moving those airlines into the main terminal April 1. The site is needed for new taxiways and the airport’s construction program to grow.

However, the airport’s 2025 passenger totals show how lightly those three gates were compared with the main terminal:

Frontier carried 553,311 passengers and Allegiant 218,043. Each South Terminal gate handled about 42% as many passengers as a main terminal gate. Moving those flights into an already crowded building wasn’t ideal, but losing three of 37 nominal gates didn’t mean losing 8% of the airport’s passenger capacity. There are actually three different construction stories here:

So commenters suggesting “reopen the closed gates” aren’t familiar with the airport. This is space being used to build out the airport.

Terminal width matters, too. Boarding lines, arriving passengers and people walking to other gates all compete for the same floor space. Austin’s master plan identified 89,600 square feet of circulation corridors after the 2019 east expansion, compared with a modeled requirement of 125,350 square feet at 16 million annual passengers and 173,650 at 22 million (almost twice the space).

Atlanta’s Concourse D project is a good contrast because it widens the building from 60 feet to 99 feet, increases the depth of gate waiting areas from 20 feet to 35 feet, and reduces the gate count from 40 to 34, with all remaining gates accommodating larger aircraft. Hold passenger traffic constant and passengers per gate rises nearly 18% simply because the denominator shrank—even as passengers get more space.

An airport can have fewer gates, higher passengers per gate, and a substantially less density for a better experience walking through the terminal.

The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid.

I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens.

They are all waiting for the single lavatory .

I think Austin feels crowded because the TSA checkpoint doesn’t have much space in front of it – people are looped back to the front of the airport. Also, IAD A/B are practically empty much of the time, and don’t even feel full when the international flights are leaving in the evening (except for the TK lounge), while C/D are either standing room only – blocking people trying to walk through during the banks or empty the rest of the time.

SFO and ATL feel so different, though they have similar passengers per gate. ATL is always a stressful madhouse, while SFO feels like it has space.

#6003. Why I’m Especially Grateful This Year

Every year on Thanksgiving I offer a reflection on the good fortune I’ve had in travel, mile and points and to be able to interact with so many wonderful readers over the course of the year. And as difficult as the past several years have been for so many (it was in many ways a dumpster fire, and we thought nothing could match 2020 and 2021) – and as tough as the coming year may be, I’m even more thankful than I’ve ever been. I’m thankful for my family’s health. I’m also thankful for the way I’ve been able to grow through challenging times. The growth I’m most pleased with is as a dad. And I’m extremely grateful for my readers. I get to interact with brilliant and thoughtful people through this blog. Sure, the comments on posts often descend into madness (it’s the internet, and I’ve been forced to delete more comments than I used to and still don’t delete nearly enough) but I’ve gotten to know so many people. I’ve been practicing at it since the start of this blog in 2002, and really going back to my BBS days in the mid-1980s. If there’s one thing I think I have to offer writing for nearly 25 years here, it’s a memory. I remember when things have happened before, been promised before, and how they worked out. And I try to offer some of that context to the day’s developments. I remember most of the people I’ve had the good fortune to get to know since I began in miles and points, and it’s sustained me throughout the years and throughout both good times and difficult times. I thought I’d take the Thanksgiving opportunity to express my thankfulness for each of you that reads my blog and interacts with me throughout the year. I’ve said this many times before but I really do consider myself one of the luckiest people, and certainly much more fortunate than I could have ever imagined. I’m deeply shy, which some people can find off-putting when I meet them (thinking that by not being outgoing with them I must not be interested, or somehow aloof). I’ve talked about my being a bit on the spectrum. The written form has allowed me to connect so well with many. And I’m grateful for those connections, although I don’t share nearly as much detail that’s personal many of you know me very well from my writing — certainly my opinions, my quirks, my sense of humor. This hobby has enriched my life in so many ways, including less obvious ones. In many ways this is still the same personal blog I first started, I write and share what is interesting to me. I usually write as though no one is reading, and I’m shocked when I get a call from an airline’s or hotel’s communications shop because a C-level executive is unhappy with something I’ve said. (Or when one of those C-level folks comments here or drops me a note, as happens so often too.) Now there are a whole lot more people reading the blog than when I started and I appreciate each and every one of you. Even the ones that are trying to insult me! I don’t always have as thick a skin as I should, but I try my best, because each and every reader has something to teach me or challenge me. And the positive feedback touches me deeply. So thank you. Thank you. I look forward to continuing to share this journey together, and I appreciate this opportunity to reflect — and to acknowledge. Topics on this pageBloggingFrequent-flyer programThanksgiving More From View from the Wing

I’m thankful for my family’s health. I’m also thankful for the way I’ve been able to grow through challenging times. The growth I’m most pleased with is as a dad.

And I’m extremely grateful for my readers. I get to interact with brilliant and thoughtful people through this blog. Sure, the comments on posts often descend into madness (it’s the internet, and I’ve been forced to delete more comments than I used to and still don’t delete nearly enough) but I’ve gotten to know so many people. I’ve been practicing at it since the start of this blog in 2002, and really going back to my BBS days in the mid-1980s.

If there’s one thing I think I have to offer writing for nearly 25 years here, it’s a memory. I remember when things have happened before, been promised before, and how they worked out. And I try to offer some of that context to the day’s developments. I remember most of the people I’ve had the good fortune to get to know since I began in miles and points, and it’s sustained me throughout the years and throughout both good times and difficult times.

I thought I’d take the Thanksgiving opportunity to express my thankfulness for each of you that reads my blog and interacts with me throughout the year. I’ve said this many times before but I really do consider myself one of the luckiest people, and certainly much more fortunate than I could have ever imagined.

I’m deeply shy, which some people can find off-putting when I meet them (thinking that by not being outgoing with them I must not be interested, or somehow aloof). I’ve talked about my being a bit on the spectrum. The written form has allowed me to connect so well with many. And I’m grateful for those connections, although I don’t share nearly as much detail that’s personal many of you know me very well from my writing — certainly my opinions, my quirks, my sense of humor. This hobby has enriched my life in so many ways, including less obvious ones.

In many ways this is still the same personal blog I first started, I write and share what is interesting to me. I usually write as though no one is reading, and I’m shocked when I get a call from an airline’s or hotel’s communications shop because a C-level executive is unhappy with something I’ve said. (Or when one of those C-level folks comments here or drops me a note, as happens so often too.)

Now there are a whole lot more people reading the blog than when I started and I appreciate each and every one of you. Even the ones that are trying to insult me! I don’t always have as thick a skin as I should, but I try my best, because each and every reader has something to teach me or challenge me. And the positive feedback touches me deeply.

So thank you. Thank you. I look forward to continuing to share this journey together, and I appreciate this opportunity to reflect — and to acknowledge.

#6002. Your Flight Takes 10 Minutes Longer Than It Used To—And That’s A Luxury Worth Paying For

Flying takes longer than it used to – and, retirement of the Concorde notwithstanding, it’s not because planes aren’t as fast. There are more than twice as many commercial flights as there were at the time of airline deregulation, and air traffic control hasn’t been upgraded very much. There’s congested airspace and also congested airports. We also don’t build major new airports – the last one was Denver, 30 years ago. (Austin’s new 1999 airport was a converted military base, and there were others like that in the 90s.) By one estimate flights have gotten 8% longer. That means a two hour flight is 10 minutes longer than it used to be. And the single biggest factor is often tagged as strategic padding of schedules. Airlines are often chided for ‘schedule padding’ – claiming that flights take longer than they should. Often, this just reflects the reality of telling customers when they can expect to arrive – although there’s greater variance than there used to be, which isn’t great for having a gate available when you land early. Airlines do not like this! Though real airfares (even including fees) are down significantly since deregulation, longer flight times are expensive for staffing, fuel and efficient use of $50 – $100 million planes. And longer travel times historically disadvantaged an airline trying to sell tickets, because it meant their flights were displayed lower on the screen that travel agents and later passengers directly saw – which translates into fewer sales. A new study finds that airlines with more “padding” in their schedules tend to charge higher fares. That sounds like passengers paying more for a slower trip. But those extra minutes can also let United hold your plane with ConnectionSaver and get you home that night, and still arrive on time. It also means fewer delays and missed connections. So that ‘premium’ is actually a more valuable product to many consumers. I’ve argued for years that schedule padding often isn’t really padding. Sometimes an airline is finally admitting how long the trip takes. Customers can plan around an honest arrival time. There’s a new chapter by Embry-Riddle’s Jules Yimga, “The Price of Punctuality,” in The Economics of Airline Pricing. It combines 2019 flight time data with the government’s ticket price survey. It compares schedules against different percentiles of actual flight times, then examines how the resulting measures relate to fares. More padding is associated with higher fares, especially when the comparison uses the faster end of actual flight times. The relationship appears in both competitive and concentrated markets. The abstract itself allows that reliability could be a service customers value. (Interestingly, Yimga’s earlier research on schedule padding attributed higher prices primarily to higher costs rather than higher margins.) Even scheduling to the median arrival time means roughly half of trips take longer than published. It’s often better for a customer if an airline underpromises and overdelivers – or arrives ‘on time’ rather than late. Predictability matters when you’re scheduling connections or trying to arrive in time for a meeting. An airline that leaves little buffer is going to appear less reliable, so customers book earlier flights and longer layovers or even fly in the night before an important meeting. Then the buffer hasn’t disappeared, it just changes who’s scheduling it. That’s why I argued American’s investment in more realistic schedules could pay for itself. Avoiding rebooking, mishandled bags and aircraft and crews getting out of position can justify spending running an on-time schedule even before a customer chooses the airline again because the trip met expectations. American’s Dallas – Fort Worth overhaul that began in April combined longer scheduled flight times with a move from nine daily banks of flights to thirteen. Spreading flights into smaller waves reduced congestion that made some of the extra time unnecessary. One plane waiting for a gate can delay its passengers, its next departure, and other flights whose crews are stuck on board. Giving the operation room to recover can prevent that problem from cascading. In January, I covered American network planning chief Brian Znotins explaining that bookings for 40–54 minute connections at DFW were 4% below what its model predicted. Bookings for 55–84 minute connections were 8% above prediction. Customers have actually started choosing longer connections because they feel more reliable and less likely to leave them stranded. When I covered United’s media day in 2019, Greg Hart explained that 25% of its flights each day were expected to arrive ten minutes early. That gave United room to use ConnectionSaver to hold flights for connecting passengers and still arrive on time. Of course there’s such a thing as too much slack. An airline can improve its reported punctuality by moving the promised arrival later without getting anyone anywhere sooner. Excessively long connections waste customer time. And routinely beating an absurdly generous schedule doesn’t make an operation excellent. Not all padding is something customers will pay a premium for. #6000. SEC Proposes Reforms to Shareholder Democracy

A potential victory for government restraint and the virtues of federalism

Outside the Securities and Exchange Commission headquarters in Washington, D.C., May 12, 2021

Every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots. Those proposals have become more controversial and divisive over time. The last several years of battles over “woke capitalism” and its inevitable backlash were largely fought through the shareholder resolution process. Now the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is about to rewrite the rules for what makes it onto those shareholder ballots, and that could mean a reset for how politics impacts corporate America — and vice versa.

Unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades. Originally implemented in 1942 and amended multiple times since, the rule gave the SEC the power to referee which ideas corporate boards need to put up for a vote and which ones they can safely ignore. But the SEC is now proposing to repeal the rule entirely, leaving those decisions up to state governments and individual companies.

Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

Alec Mena is a research fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

#5999. Trump, while wielding veto threat, sees possible deals with incoming Dem majority

President Donald Trump, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gestures during a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump said Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.

After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.

Speaking in a stuffy James A. Brady Briefing Room for just shy of 90 minutes, the GOP president contended, without naming a single Democratic leader or lawmaker, that members of the opposition party have called him “about two things in particular,” pointing to health care and immigration.

“What's happened is I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he said of the 17 days since Democrats gained dozens of seats across the two chambers. “But people that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me.”

But Trump also reminded Democrats that he is more than willing to veto legislation he doesn’t agree with, calling it one of the “extreme powers” of his office and one he might use to bring them to the bargaining table.

“So they’re going to send things my way, and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things, and I’m going to veto them,” he said. “I think, after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ’I’m going to veto, unless you want to do this and this and this.”

He predicted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely new speaker of the House, and Sen. Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., expected to become majority leader, would seek deals because both are “smart.” He would not say if he’d spoken to either leader, but called Jeffries “streetwise,” while noting he had once made a donation to Schumer earlier in their careers.

Trump went as far as to suggest working across the aisle on health care “may be easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation,” a reference to a fast-track process that allows sprawling bills to pass each chamber with a simple majority — legislation typically needs 60 votes to advance in the Senate.

The sports-loving president added the Senate-approved “Protect College Sports Act” to his list, and repeated his support for legislation to make Hollywood production companies more competitive. The House moved closer Friday to acting on an amended “Protect” bill when the Rules Committee posted a notice calling for any desired floor amendments by noon on Wednesday.

“We have to pass that bill,” Trump said. “Every college is going to go bankrupt if we don't get a bill because they're going crazy.”

The Senate’s “Protect” bill would establish the first federal regulatory framework for college athletics, setting national rules for name, image and likeness deals and compensation, as well as installing limitations on agents. It would put in place standards for NIL agreements, create guidelines for schools making direct payments to athletes and provide targeted antitrust protections to certain governing organizations.

He said the Senate bill has “tremendous bipartisan support,” but its path in the House remains unclear, according to lobbyists who have worked on the issue. That’s because some House conservatives oppose it and the Congressional Black Caucus has said its members would vote “no.”

The CBC has linked it to GOP efforts to redistrict majority minority districts in states the group, with its nearly 60 House members, contends would benefit most from the bill. The CBC is expected to be even larger in the next Congress, further complicating the “Protect” bill’s path to Trump’s desk.

Trump also pointed to the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act as another possible bipartisan bill. The legislation would establish a federal tax credit to encourage film and television productions to shoot in the United States rather than overseas. Some countries offer American film companies lucrative production incentives to shoot on their soil.

In a twist, Trump noted Sen. Adam B. Schiff — a longtime foe from the California Democrat’s days probing the president’s alleged ties to Russia as House Intelligence Committee chair during Trump 1.0 — supports that measure.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support. I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’”

But the president’s vision of a 120th Congress bipartisan agenda differs from what Democrats have promised.

Many Democratic incumbents and candidates promised voters they would pursue legislation to lower consumer prices, pare health care costs and end Trump’s Iran conflict, which the president again on Friday acknowledged hurt his party by increasing prices.

Jeffries, during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, pointed to reversing the administration’s Medicaid cuts, reviving the Affordable Care Act credits, ending the war and lowering costs as his conference’s “North Star” priorities. This week he also said he would seek to move an immigration-related bill “immediately,” and that the House would “hold the crooks accountable,” a nod to aggressive oversight both chambers are likely to engage in.

On Iran, reporters pressed Vice President JD Vance over his post-midterms X post blaming the war for the GOP wipeout. One reporter pressed Vance, a potential 2028 Republican presidential hopeful, whether he — like Trump — would start the conflict again. Vance sidestepped as he approached the lectern from behind Trump’s right shoulder, but did not give a full-throated endorsement to go to war again.

“The president has said he would do it again,” Vance replied. “And my view is that my goal is, and my job is to support the president of the United States.”

In a potential 2028 GOP primary preview, Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who has gained ground in some polls since the midterms — was expressionless as he stood a few feet away, positioned behind Trump’s left shoulder.

Trump’s midday press conference marked his first since voters handed Democrats at least 258 House seats and 56 in the Senate come Jan. 3. He again contended the outcome would have been different “if I were on the ballot,” and floated vague conspiracy theories about some falling prices since Democratic candidates bulldozed across the country.

At one point, he decided to make an announcement that he claimed he had not warned his staff about by floating a threat to U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas.

​"We're going to put a tremendous tax on them, if they do it," he said, continuing his advocacy of erecting the unpopular facilities across the United States and willingness to use executive powers.

As he returned to Washington Thursday night, the White House touted on social media what it called $17 billion in new deals secured with Asian countries this week. Trump on Friday claimed he told Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his country would begin buying “100 percent” of its oil from the United States — and Marcos had said, “Yes, sir.”

White House aides handed out a one-page “declaration toward peace” before Trump arrived that he later said he had reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The three leaders agreed to ramp up production of petroleum products, pursue unspecified changes to the United Nations and a statement that a “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” according to the White House’s description of the declaration.

It also included a line about agreement on the “principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials,” an apparent show of support to Putin being targeted by international criminal entities over his conduct of his war with Ukraine. The U.S. president on Friday said such entities have “fake power.”

Trump called the declaration “formal,” as he lauded Chinese cities he was driven through this week as extremely “clean.” He compared them to some Democratic-run U.S. cities and states he described as “so embarrassing” and “dirty.” He dubbed Xi, considered by many Republican and Democratic lawmakers to be a dictator, a “great man.”

Some Republican lawmakers who will return for the 120th Congress said they have some reservations about Trump meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, doubting Putin’s and Xi’s sincerity about changing course on a number of issues.

Retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., went further Thursday.

“Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and to China. And we stood up for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values,” Bacon, who has floated a potential 2028 presidential bid, said during a National Press Club event. “President Trump has been terrible on this right here."

“He has played footsie with Putin, he’s even blaming Zelenskyy for why the war started,” he added, referring to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “It infuriates me. And Ronald Reagan is rolling in his grave. … And now the Democrats are talking about the bad Russians and the bad Chinese, and we got to be tougher — it’s another role reversal, here.”

#5998. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Your Questions Answered

Questions from attendees. Answers by Skift Intelligence.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S. airline revenue architecture, and it’s now at the crowded end of its growth curve. Premium cabins generated $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue, in 2024, and U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy. The open question is no longer demand. It’s whether every carrier scaling premium at once dilutes the yields that made it work. 12

The behavior behind it is capital, not talk. United ordered more than 250 aircraft with more business class and premium economy, Delta is spending $1 billion on new Delta One suites arriving in early 2027, American is flying retrofitted 777-300ERs, Alaska is adding business class on widebodies and select narrowbodies plus its first premium economy, and JetBlue is launching domestic first class 345.

The results follow the spend. Delta’s premium cabins hit 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024, with premium revenue up about 57% over that stretch to $6.9 billion 6. Delta held a 9.5% operating margin through the fuel shock on fares, premium mix, loyalty, and non-flying revenue 7.

Premium is also being unbundled, which is the clearest sign it has become normal pricing infrastructure rather than a flagship product. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, extending segmentation it already applied to Polaris and Premium Plus 8. United CFO Michael Leskinen said “all of society is becoming more premium,” citing hotels, cruise lines, and car service 9.

The front cabin keeps growing but stops being one product. Tiered business fares let carriers sell the seat to price-sensitive buyers without discounting the full experience, which protects yield as capacity rises.

Skift Research’s main caution is oversupply rather than demand weakness. If carriers scale premium simultaneously, especially long-haul, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to trade up and dilute the premium.

With jet fuel averaging $4.50 a gallon and domestic fares up about 32% year over year, carriers without premium and loyalty levers are the exposed ones. Deutsche Bank expects American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier to lose money in 2026.

Premium demand in the U.S. is structural, built on a K-shaped income recovery and self-funded leisure travelers rather than corporate accounts alone. What’s cyclical is the return on it, and that depends on how much premium seating the industry adds from here.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The U.S. market supports two fully funded premium airlines today — Delta and United — and a contested third seat that American, Alaska, and JetBlue are all spending into at the worst possible moment. Premium demand is real and large, but Skift Research warns the risk ahead is oversupply, not weak demand. Fuel at record levels is deciding who can keep paying for the buildout. 921

Premium cabins generate $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue, and Delta drew 50% of passenger revenue from premium in the second quarter 3. United has grown premium seat capacity 46% since 2019, closing on Delta’s lead 5. The economics behind the third seat are much weaker: Deutsche Bank expects Delta, United, Southwest, and Allegiant to be profitable in 2026, while American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier lose money — American and JetBlue by roughly $1 billion pretax each 2.

Sources: Q3 margins and revenue growth 6; American’s results 1; Alaska’s losses and premium plan 78; JetBlue’s first class 2.

Two carriers are monetizing premium; three more are buying the seats and hoping the returns arrive. Skift Research classifies premium as a peaking trend whose main forward risk is yield dilution if everyone scales at once — which is close to what is happening now.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Loyalty cash isn’t going away — Delta took $8.2 billion from Amex in 2025 and Air Canada just had Aeroplan valued at C$10 billion, more than the airline itself. But the economics are less proven than the headline numbers suggest, the regulatory and AI risks are real, and premium cabins are now the faster-growing engine at $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue. 135

Two things are true at once. The cash from banks is enormous and disclosed; the net profit behind it is not. United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the “credit card company that happens to fly planes” framing, arguing analysts count what banks pay for miles but ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers — “Nobody counts the cost,” he said 1. Skift’s review of filings found American collected $6.2 billion from card and other partners, while United doesn’t publish total bank cash at all, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 7.2% of passenger miles in 2019 to 10.3% in 2025 1.

The clearest structural alternative is premium. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as a peaking trend airlines should scale now, with over 70% of travelers saying they would trade up and Delta’s premium revenue up nearly 50% since 2019 10. American’s Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 6.

The loyalty engine is being stress-tested from three directions at once: disclosure (nobody shows the net), regulation (uncapped U.S. interchange fees that the Credit Card Competition Act would put at risk), and discovery (AI making fares and benefits easier to compare). None of those kill it. All three argue against treating card remuneration as the only growth story.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American has closed a lot of product gaps on paper and almost none of the financial ones. Its premium seat mix is already high — roughly 30% of seats generating about 50% of revenue 4 — but Delta converts premium and loyalty into profit at a scale American doesn’t approach 1.

CEO Robert Isom now calls American a “premium global airline,” a label adopted in press releases in December 2025.

Premium drove roughly two-thirds of Delta’s passenger-revenue growth, and Delta expects premium revenue to pass main cabin by 2027.

American’s chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate returns that fund the next round of investment and pay down debt, and that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 2 3. That is the condition American hasn’t met yet.

American is closing the product gap on a timeline that runs into the early 2030s while Delta compounds the loyalty and margin advantage now. The risk is crowding: with United, Alaska, and most major international carriers expanding premium cabins at once, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to pay up, and yields come under pressure.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

The premium shift is real and durable, but it is late in its growth, not early. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as “peaking” — a trend to scale now, with oversupply rather than demand weakness as the main risk. It runs as long as capacity discipline holds and the wealth effect behind it holds. The thing that ends it is airlines all expanding the front of the plane at once, diluting yields. 12

The evidence for durability is in the revenue, not the rhetoric. Premium cabins generated $188 billion in 2024, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 1. Delta’s premium cabins reached 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024 3. Air Canada’s premium share has gone from about 20% a decade ago to roughly 30%, with a 35% target by 2030 4. The addressable market widened beyond corporate accounts: Skift Research found more than 70% of travelers say they would trade up, with self-funded leisure travelers driving the growth 1.

The supply response is where the clock starts. U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy 1. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft 5. Virgin Atlantic is taking refurbished 787s from 192 economy seats to 127 and removing its onboard bars for more premium seats 67. Turkish Airlines is adding premium economy in 2028, leaving Qatar and Etihad among the few long-haul holdouts 3. Alaska is adding premium economy for the first time even after fuel wiped out first-half profit 8.

Unbundling the front cabin keeps yields up without adding seats. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, following Delta, JetBlue, Etihad, Air France, KLM, and Qatar. Air Canada has unbundled business and premium economy and sells legroom in economy.

ZS’s Kunal Shah said the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

Premium is now a baseline revenue assumption rather than a stopgap, so the question is no longer whether it lasts but who gets squeezed when everyone’s retrofits land at once. The carriers that survive the dilution will be the ones segmenting inside every cabin instead of just adding seats at the front.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

No contradiction. American removed international first class from its 777-300ERs to fit 70 Flagship Suites per aircraft — trading a handful of ultra-premium seats for far more business class inventory. The math favors density at the top of the cabin: premium seats are about 30% of American’s fleet and generate roughly 50% of revenue, and premium revenue grew 22.9% in Q3 versus 19.5% in main cabin. 758

American announced the first class removal back in 2022, framing it then as paying for a 30% increase in premium seats on the 777s and a 63% increase on the 787-9s 8. The retrofitted 777-300ERs now flying carry 70 business class seats 4. International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air New Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

The real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate the returns that fund further improvements and pay down debt 3.

Eliminating first class is how American funds business class scale — the question is whether a carrier losing money this year can out-invest Delta and United for the same premium travelers.

The industry is moving the same direction. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft, while reducing first class from 14 suites to 12 6. Virgin Atlantic is replacing its onboard bars with more premium seats 2. Skift Research puts premium cabin revenue at $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 6.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

Tilting schedules toward high-yield local traffic in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago is a margin repair, not a differentiator. Those are exactly the markets Delta and United defend hardest, and American is attacking them with the weaker balance sheet. The local-market tilt only differentiates if it is paired with the reliability and premium product American has promised but not yet delivered fleetwide. 12

Chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that American is tailoring schedules toward higher-yield local markets in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago, while leaning on alliance partners to extend global reach 1. Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

The local-market tilt is a yield lever American controls, which is why it is being pulled. The uncertainty is whether it can hold corporate and premium local share in three cities where it is the number two or number three carrier, while slowing growth to protect 2027 profitability.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

New York is where the gap between the big three is clearest, and Skift’s reporting shows three different postures rather than three comparable expansion programs.

American’s disclosed JFK plans are schedule and product additions, not a terminal program. Summer 2027 brings JFK–Nice and more Heathrow flying alongside new Philadelphia and Charlotte transatlantic routes.

Delta co-financed its own Terminal 4 expansion with the Port Authority’s broader $18.9 billion JFK overhaul, giving it fixed infrastructure control at the airport.

United has no JFK slot portfolio of its own. The Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue, cleared by the DOT in July 2025, gives it borrowed access from Terminal 6, plus a net-neutral swap of eight Newark timings.

American’s JFK position sits inside a broader catch-up effort. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion, and is on track to lose money in 2026 1. Its New York investment is showing up in aircraft and cabins — the A321XLR with 20 Flagship Suites, the 777-300ER with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seating — rather than in gates 21.

Delta’s advantage is structural. Its Terminal 4 expansion let it consolidate all JFK flying in one facility, within an $18.9 billion airport redevelopment that also produced the new Terminal 1 and Terminal 6 34.

United’s return is the newest variable. Seven daily round trips is small, but it ends an absence at JFK and comes without United buying slots 5. United’s CFO said this week that the Blue Sky relationship stops short of a deal, pointing to JetBlue’s nearly $10 billion debt load 6.

Skift’s coverage does not include a disclosed long-term American gate or terminal program at JFK comparable to Delta’s Terminal 4 investment. Treat American’s JFK plan as route and product-level on the current record.

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

Shares are gross cash from bank partners, not profit.

Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson put the number on the record himself: co-branded credit cards are about 5% of Allegiant’s revenue, against roughly 15% at the legacy carriers and above that at Alaska and Southwest 1. He called closing that gap the airline’s biggest revenue catalyst, with more detail promised at an investor day 1.

Apply that 5% to Allegiant’s actual revenue base and you get the realistic dollar figure. The company posted $962 million in revenue in the quarter ended July 2026 and $943 million in the prior quarter, a run rate near $3.7 billion including Sun Country, which Allegiant bought for $1.5 billion and closed in May 1. That implies roughly $175 million to $190 million a year in card remuneration. The program had 600,000 cardholders and first-quarter remuneration up 9% 1. For context, Allegiant’s chief marketing officer said the Bank of America deal brought in $100 million in 2022, just over 4% of $2.3 billion in revenue 2.

The structural reason leisure carriers sit at 4% to 6% rather than 15% is spend frequency. Sun Country’s then-CMO estimated a typical customer flies once every 12 to 18 months, which is why discounters pitch the card as a way to stay relevant between trips 8.

Treat 5% to 7% of total revenue as the realistic planning band for a primarily-leisure U.S. carrier, and 10% to 15% as the legacy ceiling Allegiant is aiming at rather than a near-term forecast. Also note these are gross cash from banks, not margin — United’s Scott Kirby argues analysts count the payments and ignore the cost of carrying award passengers, and no carrier discloses that cost 3.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

Points stop being a moat once an agent can price them. What holds a member is what an algorithm can’t compare: recognition at the property or gate, reliable operations, and redemption the member can actually get. Skift Research found loyalty affiliation ranked last as a reason to trust an AI recommendation, while 83% of U.S. travelers say better personalization would make them switch programs. 21

The pressure is already measurable. Skift Research found 44% of U.S. travelers book outside their preferred program because prices are cheaper elsewhere, and 55% would follow an AI tool to a better deal 1. Among business travelers, consistently good service outranks rewards as a reason to return, 46% to 15%, and 62% say they are likely to switch for a better price or experience 3. Card programs have also taken the top of the rankings: 32% of travelers named credit cards and banks the most rewarding loyalty programs, ahead of hotels at 26% and airlines at 20% 4.

The open question is whether recognition and service can be made legible to an agent. Google’s agentic hotel booking passes along only name, payment, occupancy, and property, keeping the conversation that produced the booking — which leaves the differentiators that matter most invisible at the moment of choice. AI referrals still sit below 2% at Booking and Marriott, per Bernstein, so the terms are being set while volume is small.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

For airlines, yes — so far. Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23

The shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under new silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

The profitability of spend-based status is asserted more often than it is proven. United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

No cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1

U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12

Where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and said explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

The lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

Nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Big Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he says he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15

This is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He said chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

JetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

The parts of JetBlue’s current plan that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

One caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a new entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13

The squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

Breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 showed 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

Neeleman said Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

The commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Big Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

Scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Big Four skip.

Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

Neeleman said majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

The practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman said the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

The second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

Reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman said helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the company’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

Breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has said directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Big Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13

Breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into big cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and said chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

Breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman plans a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its new routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Big Four.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%. The constraint is that a mostly domestic, Sun Belt-weighted network of that size dilutes yield faster than cabin retrofits lift it. American earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion. 321

Scale is not disqualifying by itself. American’s premium revenue grew faster than main cabin last quarter, 22.9% against 19.5% 2. The issue is what the rest of the airline costs. Revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion in the third quarter while operating costs rose 19.7%, leaving a 1% operating margin against Delta’s 9% and United’s 7% 6.

The catch-up list is real and expensive: Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, seatback screens returning, A321XLR Europe routes in summer 2027, 777-300ERs with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seats, and Citi as sole co-brand card issuer 13. At least 50 announced changes since early 2025 1.

The unresolved question is whether premium spending generates enough cash to fund the next round. American’s CCO Nat Pieper said consistent service, network, and loyalty revenue have to produce returns that pay for further improvements and reduce debt — and that reliability is the precondition. Skift’s reporting does not yet show those returns at scale. 45

Network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty all have to be working in concert.

— Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines, at Skift Aviation Forum 5

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

Allegiant, now merged with Sun Country, serves 42 markets from Fort Lauderdale but only marginally targets former Spirit routes — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City. It is instead adding unique markets no one else flies, expanding the airport’s destination menu.

JetBlue is Fort Lauderdale’s largest carrier and treats it as the third leg of a stool with New York and Boston, adding Mint transcons, domestic first class, and a possible lounge.

The short answer: Allegiant mostly doesn’t compete with JetBlue at FLL head-to-head. It competes around it.

After Spirit shut down in May 2026, JetBlue, Frontier, Breeze, and Allegiant all added capacity at Fort Lauderdale 1. JetBlue went after Spirit’s routes directly, launching 11 new Fort Lauderdale routes on Spirit’s shutdown weekend plus a status match for Free Spirit members 3. Allegiant took a different line: of its 42 Fort Lauderdale markets, only five — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City — were Spirit cities, and it is chasing unique markets instead 1.

That reflects the two models. Allegiant flies low-frequency leisure routes from smaller cities where it is often the only nonstop, so it avoids the daily-frequency, loyalty-driven markets JetBlue serves. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale is built around Northeast traffic, Caribbean and Latin connections — more than 20 routes to Latin America — and premium: Mint lie-flat on transcons to Los Angeles and Las Vegas, with management calling the city “Florida’s biggest premium market” 1. JetBlue is also adding its BlueFirst domestic first class and weighing a Fort Lauderdale lounge 4.

Fort Lauderdale seats excluding Spirit were scheduled up a combined 40% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2026. If demand doesn’t absorb that, the thin unique routes Allegiant favors are the easiest to cut — and JetBlue, which is funding startup losses on new routes while chasing a turnaround, has the most capital at risk.

This question was addressed to Sara Nelson, International President, Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO.

Customer experience and labor-as-cost coexist only when the service promise matches the cost model. The carriers now cutting hardest — KLM, Icelandair, Alaska — are protecting margin under a fuel shock, not reinventing service. The real test is where the cuts land: outsourced ground and contact-center work, and regional crews paid about half mainline, is where the customer actually meets the airline. 326

The fuel shock is forcing the trade-off into the open. Jet fuel was up 102% year over year in mid-September, and record revenue has not covered it 4. American grew revenue 19.3% in Q3 and still posted a 1% operating margin because costs grew 19.7%; Delta and United each slipped about two points 6. Carriers that already settled big contracts — United’s five-year flight attendant deal carries a 31% pay increase and $741 million in retroactive pay — are paying for premium service with loyalty and premium-cabin cash, not by squeezing crew 45.

The unresolved question is whether outsourcing the customer-facing layer — catering, ground handling, contact centers — shows up in the service metrics airlines sell against. KLM has disclosed the cost target and the job moves; it has not disclosed a service standard tied to them.

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

India’s fleet orders are not the binding constraint — ground and crew capacity are. Mumbai is rationing international slots to rebuild a terminal, new airports rather than bigger ones are being asked to absorb growth, and tighter pilot duty rules exposed how thin airline crew buffers were. The result: capacity now gets added where slots and crews exist, not where demand is. 1167

Mumbai International Airport told 46 airlines it would pull 265 of Terminal 2’s 770 weekly international departure slots from October 25 to house domestic flights displaced by the Terminal 1 rebuild — IndiGo losing 74 weekly departures, Air India 33, Emirates and Etihad 10 each 1. The ministry intervened, Adani agreed to leave winter slots untouched, and traffic balancing was pushed to the summer 2027 schedule 23. IndiGo and Air India Group then agreed to phase international flying to Navi Mumbai through July 2027 4. The relief valve carries its own friction: Navi Mumbai is 45 km away with no direct metro link expected before 2031, and charges INR 1,225 in passenger fees against INR 615 at Mumbai 4. Adani’s airport CEO expects one or two foreign carriers to suspend Mumbai service for a couple of years rather than split operations 5.

IndiGo canceled more than 1,200 flights after new crew rostering rules collided with thin staffing and system congestion, and the DGCA opened a probe 6. The meltdown deepened — the government rolled back night-flying rules, capped fares, and fined the airline, and it cost IndiGo both profit and its CEO 789. The regulator has since shown it will flex duty rules when airspace disruption lengthens sectors, temporarily relaxing pilot duty-time limits in April 2026 10. Regulators also tied summer schedule approvals to aircraft actually on the ground rather than projected deliveries, forcing airlines to cut planned flying 11.

Skift’s reporting has tracked recruitment to beat an air traffic control officer shortage, with 796 ATC positions created alongside the fleet build-out 12, and CAPA has called for airspace redesign to carry 8–10 times current traffic 13. The sharper near-term airspace problem is geopolitical: Pakistani and Iranian closures pushed IndiGo to suspend Copenhagen and cut UK flying 14, and have hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, moving Air India’s Europe and North America flying toward Mumbai with Bengaluru under study as a third hub 15.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.
