#5883. The Model Middle Power

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America. This essay is adapted from his forthcoming book South Korea’s Grand Strategy: Narratives and the Rise of a Global Nation.

What South Korea Gets Right About Geopolitics

In the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent. In his remarks, Carney stressed that although the old U.S.-led alliance system was collapsing, middle powers—states that do not have the ability to reshape global politics but that still possess substantial might—were well positioned to pick up the slack. But to do so, Carney argued, they would need to build up their “strength at home” and “act together” to harness their collective power, even in the absence of backing from the world’s hegemon.

Although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious. They noted, correctly, that it would be very difficult for middle powers to build a grand alliance composed of countries as diverse as Brazil, Canada, South Africa, and Turkey. “The path to unity among middle powers is fraught because this group includes rich and poor countries, as well as small and large ones,” wrote the economist Eswar Prasad in February. Carney, however, is right that middle powers have an opportunity to thrive going forward. Even when aligning with great powers, these countries can still exercise greater autonomy by developing national capacity and diversifying external partnerships.

South Korea offers a prime example of this flexible approach. For decades, Seoul has pursued a middle-power strategy centered on building domestic strength and forging partnerships with democracies everywhere while deepening its alliance with Washington. South Korea has been adaptable, recalibrating its security alignments, economic strategies, and diplomatic roles as regional and global conditions require. This has enabled a country smaller in size than most of the world’s states to punch far above its weight, exercising substantial influence in Asia and beyond.

Not every government can follow Seoul’s path, and South Korea’s strategy has its limits. As Seoul itself acknowledges, middle powers cannot escape great-power competition. But the country has begun to show what middle powers can accomplish when they leverage their partnerships and their own strength to protect their interests and deter larger threats. And by maintaining and even building its ties to the United States while asserting greater autonomy, South Korea has proven that middle powers can strengthen themselves without building whole new networks—contrary to Carney’s suggestion.

According to classic international relations theory, grand strategy is the exclusive provenance of great powers. The United States’s effort to contain the Soviet Union during the Cold War is a paradigmatic example; China’s pursuit of global economic primacy is another. Middle powers, by contrast, have little say in such strategies. Instead, these countries are seen as primarily reactive in their foreign policies, navigating around the decisions of the great powers rather than setting the agenda themselves.

But recent history suggests that the division between great and middle powers is less clear-cut than has been assumed. In practice, middle powers very much have their own affirmative visions that they pursue in the world. They have the leeway to decide which threats matter most to them, which partnerships to prioritize, and where to invest scarce resources. Japan, concerned with the threat posed by China, has been quietly exercising leadership in the Indo-Pacific by improving its ties with neighbors, increasing investment and aid to the region, and strengthening its own defense capabilities—all while remaining closely allied with the United States. India, worried about China, Pakistan, and growing economic headwinds, has successfully bolstered partnerships with the United States and other democracies but maintained its relationship with Russia.

Much like Japan and India, South Korea is worried about its neighbors. But for Seoul, this is nothing new. South Korean leaders have been concerned with the very thing Carney fretted about in his Davos speech—becoming collateral damage in conflicts between great powers— since at least the late nineteenth century, when it was caught between China, Japan, and Russia. The country has a well-known proverb, “When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken,” that captures the sentiment that great-power feuds can harm countries caught in the middle.

To safeguard against this threat, Seoul has long sought to increase its self-reliance through industrial policy. The country transited from light to heavy export industries in the 1970s, turning it into a major player in the chemical, steel, and shipbuilding sectors. State investments helped it become a major global producer of batteries and semiconductors in the present era. South Korea takes great pride in what historians call “the miracle on the Han”—or the country's rapid rise from a war-torn and impoverished state to a rich one during the late twentieth century. They now use the state’s wealth to promote public goods globally, contributing to international development, global health, climate policy, and multilateral bodies.

Seoul has also built up a formidable military, one that experts consistently rank as among the strongest in the world. Today, many South Korean analysts argue that Seoul needs a nuclear arsenal for self-defense, even though the country officially remains under Washington’s nuclear umbrella. The state has simultaneously used its armed prowess to deepen relations with U.S. allies. Seoul, for example, has inked multibillion-dollar arms deals with European buyers, making it a key partner in rebuilding NATO’s industrial capacity. In 2025, it was the second largest supplier of weapons to European NATO members (after the United States). South Korea has also forged defense partnerships in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, widening Seoul's options and reducing its dependence on any single market. South Korea, in other words, has been able to convert its economic resources and bureaucratic capabilities into greater influence by expanding its partnerships, strengthening its voice in international bodies, and helping shape global rules and norms.

But even as it charts its own path, Seoul has no plans to abandon the United States, at least in the near future. In fact, the sanctity of the U.S.-South Korean relationship is a significant historical Korean narrative. Many South Koreans see the alliance as a bond inked in blood, thanks to the sacrifice both countries made during the Korean War, when they worked to stop North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, from overrunning the south. Most South Koreans correctly believe that the continued U.S. military presence in the country—currently, 28,500 American troops are stationed on the peninsula—has played a major part in deterring North Korean aggression over the past seven decades.

At first glance, South Korea’s strategy may seem contradictory. On the one hand, the country wants to deepen its cooperation with the United States, on which it still depends for security. But on the other, it seeks greater autonomy.

Yet these twin goals are not actually at odds. By cultivating ties with Washington, Seoul has gained access to advanced military capabilities and technologies as well as a larger diplomatic platform to expand its regional and global interests. It is in part because of this relationship, for example, that South Korea has had such success at selling weapons to multiple NATO members, including Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Norway, Poland, and Romania. (Seoul has also built up a formidable diplomatic apparatus in its own right.) At the same time, South Korea helps make this compact worthwhile for the United States by providing it with valuable technology, including semiconductor chips. Seoul has also partnered with the Washington to help revive the American shipbuilding industry, agreeing to invest $150 billion in the U.S. sector.

Still, South Korea’s growing push for more independence in its foreign policy does result in some tensions with the United States that cannot easily be resolved. For instance, the current government’s push to give Seoul, not Washington, operational control over both states’ forces on the peninsula in the event of war has been rebuffed by the U.S. military. American commanders instead favor a conditions-based transfer after South Korea has proven it has the capabilities to lead a joint defense, rather than setting a fixed date. The two sides also have not reached a consensus on what role South Korea would play if Taiwan is attacked or blockaded by China.

Yet so far, Seoul has done an effective job at managing these differences. For example, in his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Washington’s allies, including South Korea, of leeching off the United States and not paying their fair share. To extract more from Washington’s partners, Trump has implemented punishing tariffs. In response, South Korea could have been defiant and slapped on retaliatory restrictions, as other U.S. allies did. Instead, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung avoided rebuking the president and worked to meet American demands in ways that heightened the two states’ mutual dependence. For instance, Lee pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States to advance American economic and national security interests, including by purchasing more U.S. military equipment, and to increase South Korean economic support for locally stationed American forces.

Seoul’s strategy has not been a uniform success. The South Korean economy remains exposed to American and Chinese pressure despite its growth and diversification. North Korea is expanding its nuclear and missile forces and deepening military ties with Russia, creating new security headaches for which Seoul still needs U.S. assistance. The country is politically polarized, resulting in sharp policy shifts that can undermine long-term strategic planning. It also suffers from the lowest birthrate of any country in the world, threatening its tax base and the size of its armed forces. Beyond that, South Korea may not provide the ideal template for every middle power. Not every country in this category has similar economic resources, networks, or ties to the United States.

But on the whole, South Korea’s grand strategy has been effective, and it thus carries broader lessons. For one, it shows how adaptive middle powers can draw on their respective national narratives to find their strengths and to chart a path forward. Perhaps more important, it is proof positive that middle powers can exercise influence and achieve a measure of autonomy even without working together to build a neutral third pole, as Carney urged. It also illustrates that middle powers can remain firmly allied with the United States while developing their own independent capabilities. South Korea, then, demonstrates that states can reduce their vulnerability and widen their political options.

An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the South Korean government was known to be considering developing nuclear weapons.

With Its Allies, Seoul Has Enough Leverage to Push Back

Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery

Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too big to fail”?

Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too big to fail”?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley tech elites or by D.C. political elites—or an entwinement between the two?

Adam Tooze: Some reporting suggests that the rally around Huang really began in Silicon Valley itself. So it was a key group of people who were close to him: Uber founder Travis Kalanick, a bunch of venture capitalists like Gavin Baker, who’s been tweeting very effusively about this, Brad Gerstner and Marc Andreessen, who we’ve discussed on the show before. Heavy hitters. Apparently, there’s some Goldman Sachs interest as well. None of those people have really been willing to comment. But there was a rallying around Jensen Huang and the need to bring him back in. I think, basically, it was a combination of their influence plus a sell-off in the market that really prompted Trump to act. The venture capitalists have good connections to [Vice President] J.D. Vance, because he had that little foray in Silicon Valley finance by way of Peter Thiel. And they seem to then have been able to act on figures inside the Trump administration. Jensen Huang is, after all, very well known to Trump. The two have been seen together a lot in public.

And then there was some last-minute fig leaf-style conversations with the attorney general just to confirm that they’re not actually supporting a figure that is currently under investigation by the American judicial authorities. So apparently the attorney general, Todd Blanche, signed off on this. And that was really then the decisive moment when Trump then intervened with the board, which seems to be a remarkably weak institution. For a company of Nvidia’s size and significance, its corporate governance is schoolyard. It comes out of the era when it was a scrappy manufacturer of accelerator chips for video games rather than the biggest company in the world and the backstop to AI. So it seems to just be this incredible kind of jury-rigged, duct tape—you know, people refer to duct-tape empire—kind of setup that we’re dealing with here. And truly dramatic in its impact then on the market, though questions are being asked, I think, about how long the rebound can really last given the underlying questions about AI and the broader economy.

CA: What are the mechanics by which a leader of the U.S. government overrides a corporate board? And are there any precedents for a U.S. president personally intervening in a boardroom decision like this?

AT: I don’t think he has very many direct levers, other than his public sway. As corporate America has demonstrated across the board during his second term, no one wants to be on his wrong side. So if he told this weak corporate governance body at Nvidia that, you know, this is the way to go, and there really were no legal objections, at least at the level of espionage, then presumably they felt it was in the shareholders’ best interest to just do as they were told. It’s not entirely without precedent.

The most recent instance would be the Obama administration’s move against the leadership of General Motors in the spring of 2009 when the federal government did a bailout for General Motors. And they removed Rick Wagoner, who they didn’t feel that they could work with. Then beyond that, you have to go further back in history to the Cold War-era presidencies. So there’s action by the [Franklin] Roosevelt administration against the Ford Motor Company leadership when they were deeply worried during the wartime about the succession of Henry Ford and deaths within the Ford family. There’s Truman intervening in the steel industry in the early 1950s. There’s a moment when Kennedy also intervenes at U.S. Steel in ’62.

But, you know, the fundamental difference here is that we’re not in a state of war. This is not a matter of urgent national security or of macroeconomic pressure like in the early 1950s during the Korean War. This isn’t the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia is not on the receiving end of a federal government bailout. You know, the analogies quite rapidly break down and leave one feeling that in some senses, this truly is an unprecedented intervention. This is the most valuable company in the world at various points. And it just basically doesn’t appear to have any serious corporate governance whatsoever.

Jensen Huang and the broader AI sector represent an enormous risk for the entire public.

The return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang exposes a dangerous gap in corporate oversight.

CA: The intervention on behalf of Jensen Huang seemed to be motivated by a sense that he was somehow essential, not only to the success of the company, but through the company, to the success of the American economy overall. In what sense could Huang be considered to be “too big to fail”?

AT: Well, that term comes out of banking. And within the banking sector, since the Dodd-Frank reforms and other global financial stability reforms in the aftermath of 2008, designations as GSIB, so globally systemically significant banks and financial institutions, are formalized and have been formalized. And they do actually have a relatively formal or quantitative definition. I mean, you can look at bank balance sheets and just trace networks of interconnection and risks that arise from those. And there’s a quite serious study of those kinds of risks. And one could do the same for Nvidia. And there has been a great deal of speculation along these lines, or not just speculation, but investigation. And it’s quite clear that the circular financing mechanisms that we’ve also discussed on the show going back awhile now all center on Nvidia. And so questions have been asked about the stability of the Nvidia financing structure.

But I think the question was always, should they not be subject to some kind of oversight? Right now, there is no risk of failure, right? In some senses this invocation of failure in the worst-case scenario—you know, she’s a spy and Nvidia is going to fail and therefore, you know, we must do x or y, or not do x or y, or bring him back or shove him out or whatever—the whole discourse is massively exaggerated. I mean, they’re a very successful tech business, which right now is in the middle of a boom in AI, which does have some bubble characteristics. But the financing of this is extended and ramified, but it’s the cloud providers, not necessarily Nvidia, that anyone thought of as being immediately in trouble. And even those are some way away from outright failure. And so this, you know, this language of exigency and this language of crisis, you know, it has a historical root and there are some structural reasons why one might worry about Nvidia, but it doesn’t justify the current action one way or the other. And the fact that the company is as poorly structured as it is such that so much revolves around one man is prima-facie reason for, you know, some serious rethinking and some serious structural governance.

But that would require market pressure. And you know, the financial markets right now are bonkers. That they would reprice the company by 30 percent of a trillion dollars on the basis of this kind of news is, in itself, you know, profoundly delegitimizing. So to my mind, like, it’s an absolute disaster of American public discourse, because the allegations appear to be hugely exaggerated, the damage done to the market suggests that the corporate governance is terrible, the reporting by the American media has been shambolic, the president’s intervention is unprecedented and bonkers, and now the markets vindicate the whole thing by raising the value of Nvidia by 30 percent. I mean, it feels like everyone’s kind of lost their minds in some ways. And yet, as someone famously said, whilst the music plays, you dance. Because if you’re not on the Nvidia train, you’re not doing as well as other people. And all of these boosters are saying this is a vindication of the American success story and Jensen Huang is the latest character in that ongoing narrative. It all feels a bit delirious, to be honest.

Cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi

Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze

#5880. EXCLUSIVE: White House accuses South Korea of breaking promise to Trump as US tech giant faces $688M in fines

More than 50 House lawmakers, led by Rep. Darrell Issa, are raising alarms over what they call discriminatory South Korean policies that harm American tech companies and tilt economic advantages toward China-linked competitors.

FIRST ON FOX — The White House accused South Korea of breaking a promise to President Donald Trump to treat U.S. tech companies fairly, telling Fox News Digital that Seoul has since hit Coupang with hundreds of millions of dollars in fines.

South Korean regulators have hit Coupang with roughly $688 million in fines, including a provisional $224 million penalty against its food delivery service, which was announced this month.

A White House official said the administration opposes South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's alleged discrimination against U.S. companies and that the White House expects South Korea to keep its commitment to fair treatment for U.S. technology companies, including Coupang.

EXPLOSIVE HOUSE REPORT REVEALS SECRET OPERATION INSIDE CHINA AT CENTER OF SOUTH KOREA'S FIGHT WITH US COMPANY

President Donald Trump welcomes South Korean President Lee Jae Myung at the White House in Washington, D.C., Aug. 25, 2025. (Brian Snyder/Reuters)

A South Korean embassy official punched back at the White House's allegation that there was a direct targeting of Coupang, stating that the nation abides by the agreement with the Trump administration and is committed to a fair and nondiscriminatory business environment.

"All investigations and decisions undertaken by the Korean government, including the recent fine imposed on food delivery service providers for anticompetitive conduct by the Korean Fair Trade Commission have been conducted lawfully and in accordance with applicable laws and regulations," a spokesperson for the Embassy of the Republic of Korea told Fox News Digital. "Furthermore, the right to seek legal remedies under the Korean law is fully guaranteed."

The spokesperson explained that South Korea considers its strategic partnership with the U.S. its most important relationship, describing an alliance built on democracy, the rule of law and open markets, adding that Seoul will keep working closely with American policymakers to correct the record and deepen economic ties between the two countries.

FORMER US AMBASSADOR SAYS SOUTH KOREA PROSECUTED HIM OVER SPEECH MADE ON AMERICAN SOIL

Coupang, dubbed the "Amazon of South Korea" despite having no affiliation with Amazon, is the country's largest e-commerce company, known for its "Rocket Delivery" network that gets most orders to customers' doors the next day or even the same day.

President Donald Trump shakes hands with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung at the Gyeongju National Museum in Gyeongju, South Korea, Oct. 29, 2025. (AP)

Although nearly all its business is in South Korea, Coupang is an American company. It is incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in Seattle and listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

The company was founded in 2010 by Korean American entrepreneur Bom Kim, who dropped out of Harvard Business School.

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS

A State Department official told Fox News Digital the Korea Fair Trade Commission’s continued "assault" on American companies is threatening the broader potential of the U.S.-South Korea alliance.

The State Department said it is actively evaluating a range of policy options to respond to what it calls discriminatory treatment.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, center left, and his wife, Kim Hea Kyung, arrive to depart for China at the Seoul airport in Seongnam, South Korea, Jan. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Lee Jin-man)

Yoon Suk Yeol, of the People Power Party, was elected president in 2022 but was impeached in December 2024, largely for his attempt to declare martial law.

Lee Jae Myung, of the Democratic Party, lost to Yoon in the 2022 presidential election but was elected president in 2025. The Democratic Party holds a strong majority in South Korea’s National Assembly, giving the party control of both the presidency and the legislature for the first time since 2022.

FORMER SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT YOON SUK YEOL SENTENCED TO 30 YEARS OVER NORTH KOREA DRONE FLIGHTS

The Democratic Party is South Korea's main liberal party and favors progressive domestic policies. The country's conservatives have historically favored less engagement with North Korea and stronger ties with the U.S.

Coupang said it has been the largest source of U.S. foreign direct investment in South Korea over the past decade, a claim House Republicans repeated in an April letter to South Korea's ambassador. The company said it drove more than $5 billion in overseas sales of American goods and services in 2025.

The Coupang Inc. logo atop the company's headquarters, in Seoul, South Korea, on Dec. 15, 2025. (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA

"As we have throughout the past year, Coupang continues to seek a constructive resolution that will strengthen the U.S.-Korea alliance, accelerating trade and investment that benefits both countries," Robert Porter, Coupang Inc.'s chief global affairs officer, told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., who has been outspoken about South Korea's alleged discrimination against American companies, identified Biung-Ghi Ju, chair of the Korea Fair Trade Commission, as a key figure in the alleged practices.

TRUMP ORDERS MAJOR CUT TO US-SOUTH KOREA DRILLS AS NORTH KOREA RAMPS UP MISSILE TESTS

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., during a House Judiciary Committee field hearing in New York, on April 17, 2023. (Stephanie Keith/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"For eight decades, America and Korea have benefited from an alliance purchased by sacrifice on the battlefield, joined by economic opportunity, and bolstered by mutual values," Issa told Fox News Digital. "The Lee government has the opportunity to repair or damage our relationship, and I hope he chooses the path of friendship, rather than continued confrontation."

"But that is being put at risk by the anticompetitive policies of KFTC Chairman Ju that have unfairly targeted America’s tech industry and even individual American citizens," he added.

SOUTH KOREAN PRESIDENT JUMPS TO INVEST IN MILITARY AFTER TRUMP CUTS JOINT EXERCISES

In July, the House Judiciary Committee outlined a timeline of the South Korean government's scrutiny of Coupang, from a secret laptop recovery mission in China directed by South Korea's National Intelligence Service to the agency's request that the National Assembly pursue perjury charges against Harold Rogers, interim CEO of Coupang Corp., the company's South Korean subsidiary.

A National Assembly committee filed the complaint, but Seoul police cleared Rogers in September and declined to refer the case to prosecutors. Rogers did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, center, waves the national flag and cheers during the 80th anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule in Seoul, Aug. 15, 2025. (AP)

At the time it was published, South Korea disputed the report, saying that it was based on "unilateral assertions" made by Coupang.

"The Government of the Republic of Korea regrets that the interim staff report published by the U.S. House Judiciary Committee appears to be largely based on the unilateral assertions of Coupang and respectfully disagrees with several characterizations in the report," the embassy said.

#5879. Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.

How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones

On September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta. Within hours, militants from that organization launched a dramatic campaign of terror. The group, known colloquially as Los Pachenca, demanded that businesses across the city shutter. Some 90 percent of shops did, as videos circulated of gunmen shooting up storefronts that stayed open.

For two decades, Los Pachenca has been the unquestioned criminal authority in the beachfront city and the adjacent Sierra Nevada mountain range, charging extortion payments from businesses and residents and controlling the flow of drugs out of the Port of Santa Marta, en route to Europe and beyond. But the level of control the group exhibited during the strike was particularly jarring, given that Santa Marta is the vacation home of many of the country’s elite and a common destination for international visitors. Colombia’s government responded by militarizing the city, sending in hundreds of soldiers and police officers, who rolled into town on the main highway with tanks and air support. Many shops still stayed closed until the morning of September 25, when the group announced that it was ending the strike. For locals, Los Pachenca’s reaction was a message about who remains in charge.

Calm has since returned to Santa Marta, but the incident may be indicative of risks to come. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has promised a steep military escalation against illegal groups, which have grown precipitously in recent years. As he does so, armed and criminal organizations will undoubtedly respond. Often, their target will not be the state. Instead, they will likely direct their violence against the civilian populations, whom they have spent years coopting and coercing. That is because armed and criminal groups across the country have learned that their true leverage is their ability to govern local communities—and to intimidate and punish them into silence. Even when they do attack state forces, their use of weapons such as improvised explosives and makeshift drones means that bystanders often suffer. In one recent incident in the Pacific coast department of Valle del Cauca, four drone attacks launched by an armed group in a single day left five civilians injured.

These dangers are particularly acute as de la Espriella’s pledge of a zero-tolerance crackdown against armed and criminal groups has won enthusiastic support from Washington. Both countries want big and visible victories against these outfits. They triumphantly announced a new era of cooperation when the president took office in August, including a promise of upgraded military ties. (The United States has not yet publicly pledged new weapons, but it is already providing greater intelligence and logistical assistance on some operations.) After two years of tensions and threats between President Donald Trump and leftist former President Gustavo Petro, the political realignment means that Colombia is once again the United States’ closest defense ally in South America. This is likely to continue, despite major Democratic wins in the U.S. Congress, as the relationship’s focus on security has a long history of bipartisan support.

This week, during U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, the de la Espriella administration signaled that it would seek congressional approval for joint military operations with the United States in Colombia. This cooperation will likely yield initial results. The Colombian government has said that it aims to ramp up attacks against armed and criminal groups and to go after leaders who enjoyed protection as counterparts in peace talks during the past administration.

Yet Colombia’s true challenge is not how to carry out attacks but what to do afterward. Surgical strikes, which see the military enter and exit quickly, leave civilians more vulnerable in the aftermath, as armed groups retaliate against alleged informants and tighten their grip in areas they control. Bogotá must ensure that every operation includes contingencies to anticipate criminal groups’ reactions and build on successful offensives by weakening their grasp on communities. The government will need to strengthen the police’s ability to patrol contested areas, a costly but necessary process that the United States and other partners should support.

The stakes are high. Bogotá has a chance to leverage its increased military pressure to open the door for the state, rewriting the story of who governs conflict areas. If the government misses this opportunity to consolidate state control, however, Colombia risks entering an escalatory spiral in which civilians pay a mounting price for a campaign intended to protect them.

Armed and criminal groups have spent the last decade expanding their reach across Colombia. According to the local think tank Pares, the number of municipalities with an armed group presence rose from 212 in 2018 to 518 last year—or about half of all municipalities. This deterioration reversed dramatic and hard-won improvements in security. After the historically violent decades of the 1990s and 2000s, military pressure and negotiations yielded a 2016 peace agreement demobilizing the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), once the country’s dominant rebel group. Colombia’s countryside breathed a sigh of relief as the FARC pulled out of areas where it had been in control, which represented a quarter of the country’s land.

The FARC’s exit, however, did not pave the way for Colombia’s highly centralized and bureaucratic state to claim control of those vast geographies. Instead, old armed groups such as the National Liberation Army and newer ones such as the Gaitanista Army of Colombia (also known as the Gulf Clan) saw a chance to expand their access to trafficking routes, coca crops, illegal mines, and, ultimately, vulnerable rural populations. Kidnapping for extortion and mass displacement began to resurface, shattering optimism that progress would move in one direction. Over the last four years, membership in illegal groups has nearly doubled, to some 27,000 fighters today.

As a candidate, de la Espriella successfully harnessed public frustration by promising mano dura, or iron-fisted tactics, including aerial attacks and increased incarceration, facilitated by the construction of mega-prisons. He blamed his predecessor’s administration for accelerating insecurity. The first leftist to be elected president in modern Colombia, Petro had entered office in 2022 vowing to de-emphasize the military’s role and instead hold peace talks with various armed organizations. But not every group participated, and many of the ones that did sought to take advantage of cease-fires to cement their control over communities. Midway through his term, Petro pivoted back toward deploying the armed forces. But much of the harm was already done.

Colombia’s new president has been in office only a little more than 100 days, but the shift is marked. De la Espriella carried out three bombing raids in his first weeks. He has extradited dozens of individuals to the United States, including senior leaders, and the administration has killed or captured many others. The president is doggedly pushing to restart aerial fumigation of coca crops, which the state carried out in the early 2000s to try to reduce the number of hectares under cultivation; the practice has since been heavily restricted by court rulings over concerns about health and environmental consequences. Both in private and in public, military leaders laud the government’s new support for their operations.

The Trump administration has also welcomed these developments, which align with a regional trend favoring Washington’s approach on counternarcotics. For Colombia, the new era of security cooperation with the United States represents a return to the status quo ante of the last quarter century, which was briefly disrupted by the Petro administration. U.S.-Colombian military ties were forged through antidrug efforts and deepened in 1999 with Plan Colombia, a decadelong $10 billion aid package that funded, among other things, the expansion and professionalization of the security forces and fumigation. The Colombian police and military are deeply integrated with their American counterparts. They use U.S.- and NATO-compatible systems, travel by the hundreds to the United States each year for instruction, and receive American intelligence. In nearly every operation, at least one step (and often far more) in the logistical chain is either coordinated with Washington or relies on U.S. support. That relationship never fully stopped under Petro, but the two sides were notably wary of each other. Now bilateral trust appears to be restored.

Even before the elections, de la Espriella impressed U.S. officials by outlining his plans to reclaim security momentum for the state. The Colombian president is now acting on several explicit U.S. priorities, including extraditions and legislation to designate numerous groups as terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Bogotá’s coca eradication targets are even more ambitious than Washington’s. At a personal level, relations are strong, too. Two of Colombia’s top military officials previously served as envoys to U.S. Southern Command.

Bogotá says that it intends to deliver results for Washington’s antidrug goals and has explicitly asked for additional support in the form of funding, aircraft, surveillance technologies, and maintenance. Although Colombia’s military remains among the best trained in the region, its logistical needs are critical. Only 13 of Colombia’s 53 Black Hawk helicopters are in working order, and defense spending has shrunk as a share of the national government’s budget, from 22.4 percent in 2003 to just 14.7 percent in 2025, with a growing proportion of those funds spent on salaries and pensions.

How much the United States will provide remains to be seen. In August, U.S. Southern Command’s General Francis Donovan discussed ways to shore up the deteriorating air fleet during a visit to Bogotá. The United States has also redeployed surveillance drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, where they are already aiding intelligence collection. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reluctant to pledge specific aid while in Colombia in September, and most of this assistance is likely to be in kind or to stay in the hands of the U.S. military and contractors, with little entering the Colombian budget. Much of it appears to be focused on short-term offensive wins.

Colombia has returned to tactics such as aerial bombardment because they arguably worked against the FARC. Founded as a Marxist rebellion in the 1960s, the group behaved like a conventional army, dressed in uniforms, and sought out combat with the state. This meant that the Colombian military could bomb encampments and that capturing leaders left the organization at times rudderless. Slowly chipping away at the FARC’s hierarchy and control helped push the group to finally negotiate its disarmament, beginning in 2012.

But today, those same strategies are yielding diminishing returns. The current generation of armed and criminal groups has little interest in confronting the state. Instead, they behave like businesses, seeking to safeguard access to natural resources, supply chains, and trafficking routes. They live within the civilian population and rarely wear uniforms. Leaders are easily replaced and hierarchies are fluid. Critically, Colombia’s armed groups have learned that wars with the military are costly but that controlling local populations—through intimidation and violence, but also by offering economic incentives, jobs, and services—is comparatively cheap. The battlefield has evolved from a conventional conflict to a contest over who can govern territories and the people living there.

Santa Marta offers an example of how this new model of warfare works. On most days, an outsider in the city would never perceive the presence of Los Pachenca. The group’s members do not patrol or identify themselves. Yet residents know them well from the weekly or monthly extortion payments they are forced to make. Local companies and government officials essentially view the group as an inescapable reality. Pushing back carries a violent price, but paying a protection tax, taking a bribe, or facilitating illegal commerce keeps business running smoothly.

The criminal governance of rural areas is even more suffocating. Groups that emerged from splinters of the former FARC, known as dissidents, often force local residents to hold identity cards, issued so that militants have a full census of who lives in the area and can detect possible enemy fighters. In the Amazon region, these groups keep a land registry more complete than that of the state so that they know exactly whom and how much to extort.

With this intense surveillance over society, armed and criminal groups frequently deploy the civilian population as human shields against military offensives and police patrols. The most egregious example is the widespread use of forcibly recruited children as bodyguards for senior commanders. De la Espriella’s initial bombardments, which killed at least six children, were even temporarily halted by a court over concerns about minors. Senior officers admit that these types of casualties are inevitable around high-value targets, and that the groups know that the military is far less likely to proceed if it means killing children.

Armed and criminal groups will also try to use the military operations to their political advantage. When children are killed in bombardments, for example, FARC dissidents spin the local narrative into a story about how the state cares little for rural populations. The argument sticks because there is rarely a credible state presence that can serve and protect these same communities and earn their trust.

There are more immediate consequences, as well. In the aftermath of bombardments and high-level captures, armed and criminal groups often undertake what amounts to a purge of the population, killing or exiling anyone they believe to have collaborated with the state. And when the state takes out a leader, intra-group violence frequently ensues as former associates compete to take his place. Many residents shelter inside to avoid being caught up in the fighting, leaving children without school and parents without income. If new splinter groups emerge, the combat for control over neighborhoods can place even more civilians in the crossfire. This fallout widens the gap between immediate tactical results and long-term security gains. Taking out a senior leader wins applause, but conditions may well worsen on the ground.

De la Espriella’s administration has rightly identified winning territorial control, permanently dislodging criminal groups, and restoring state governance as its ultimate goals. The dilemma it now faces—exacerbated by U.S. support that focuses on attention-grabbing wins—is how to both achieve short-term results and ensure that these do not unleash new waves of violence, retaliation against civilians, and, in turn, criminal consolidation.

The challenge is twofold. First, the military needs to anticipate groups’ violent reactions and to safeguard the population. In the case of Santa Marta, for example, the government could have increased police presence in the city in the hours after El Cholo was killed. Before the next bombardment or high-level capture, the state should ensure that a ground team of soldiers or military police is ready to hold the ground, protect the community, and prevent the armed group from swiftly stepping back in to reclaim territory.

The second challenge—establishing lasting territorial control—is trickier. A permanent rural security presence might offer the best chance for Colombia’s government to change the direction of the conflict. The country’s military leadership controls only the tip of the spear, not the rest of the state. Time and again, governments “send only the military to the hardest areas,” a retired senior officer told Crisis Group. Moreover, soldiers are operating under heavy pressure for quick wins, which are measured in the number of combatants and especially high-value targets that are killed or captured. There is a real risk that by focusing largely on these statistics, the state will overlook more comprehensive policies necessary to achieve durable security.

Pressure to deliver fast results has in the past incentivized unacceptable practices. In the early 2000s, intense political demands for combat kills fueled elaborate schemes in which soldiers murdered thousands of civilians and counted them as guerrilla fatalities, a scandal known as “false positives.” These crimes deeply compromised public trust in the security forces, and the military has worked for years to build a culture and procedures that ensure they do not happen again. Today, the country’s senior military leadership is likely the first and best brake on any attempts to use excessive force. Commanders say that they are cognizant of the need to guard against rules being slowly stretched until they are broken. “We need a stronger security approach, but it also worries us when we hear there is pressure for ‘results,’” one officer said. But U.S. rhetoric and behavior, including its decision to sink what it claims are drug-smuggling boats on the high seas, compound these risks.

Success, then, may demand a strategy that is ultimately anchored in a much stronger and larger police force, fit for the job of safeguarding civilians rather than merely carrying out offensive strikes. Military operations can generate a window of opportunity by shuffling dynamics on the ground or removing certain dangerous players. Yet those reconfigurations will turn out in the state’s favor only if the resulting vacuum is eventually filled by reliable law enforcement. Take, for example, an operation that temporarily dislodges a group from a rural hamlet. If the military acts alone, it will likely enter and leave in a matter of days or even hours, allowing the armed group to quickly return. If, however, the offensive is followed up with permanent police patrols, access to the justice system, and social interventions, criminals will have a harder time regaining control.

This, of course, is easier said than done, given the government’s resource constraints. To create effective and permanent patrols, police departments operating in the countryside need more officers and equipment to maintain a presence in the most remote communities. Colombia has roughly 180,000 uniformed police officers, a figure that, per capita, puts it on the lower end of OECD countries, many of which are far more urbanized and therefore easier to patrol. In Colombia’s conflict-affected areas, outgunned officers must often stay inside their local stations for their own safety, limiting their ability to build trust and channels of communication with the population. Other state institutions, such as the justice system, say that they cannot establish a durable foothold in villages without guarantees of protection in the medium term—exactly what rural policing should strive to provide. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs has funded the building and equipping of rural police stations in the past; it should expand this work. International partners with long-standing expertise in rural policing, such as Canada and France, could provide critical support, as well.

In cities, the challenge is different. In Santa Marta, for example, the state is present, but it is weak and vulnerable to the pressure and cooptation of the same groups that it must confront. The police need both more officers and better working conditions—including salaries, benefits, access to education, and social support for families—that could help them resist bribes. Regular vetting and counterintelligence checks can help ensure that police are fighting on the side of the state and not its adversaries.

Expanding the police will be an expensive, long-term undertaking. In the interim, Colombia could prioritize more personnel for critical areas and ensure that officers have a strong grounding in community policing, allowing them to understand the most pressing risks facing civilians. That means regular outreach to communities to build trust and make certain that officers are seen as having a stake in local well-being. The United States, meanwhile, must continue to help Bogotá strengthen its police and courts with direct financial and technical assistance.

Colombia, backed by renewed U.S. support, cannot afford to repeat past mistakes or ignore how the conflict has changed. Bogotá must therefore plan for and capitalize on military pressure to do something no government in Colombia’s history has done: govern well in conflict areas.

Bogotá Must Do More to Stop Armed Groups From Recruiting Minors

#5877. De Gaulle and the Art of European Defiance

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Review: De Gaulle and the Art of European Defiance

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more quickly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and new.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more quickly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and new.

Each of the film’s two parts is just over two and a half hours long. The first, De Gaulle: Résistance (158 minutes; released in France as L’Age de fer), opens with the humiliation of the French collapse in June 1940. Refusing to accept the armistice, de Gaulle flees to England in a tiny plane. From there, he presses British Prime Minister Winston Churchill for greater support and builds a shaky government-in-exile from scratch, operating from a tiny office in central London.

The second, De Gaulle: Liberté (159 minutes; J’écris ton nom in France), covers 1943 to the end of 1944, following both the actions of the Resistance and de Gaulle’s power struggles with rival claimants to French leadership, before moving on to D-Day and the liberation of Paris. The epic closes movingly on Armistice Day, when Churchill visits the freed capital as de Gaulle’s guest.

For audiences outside France, some of this will be familiar, from de Gaulle’s defiant broadcasts on the BBC to his haughty and stubborn personal affect. Undeniably imperious and quite unable to forget a slight, Abkarian’s de Gaulle is both a model of determination in the face adversity and, to the Allied leaders who bankrolled him, a quintessentially French pain in the ass.

A still from De Gaulle: Résistance.Pathe Films

Other episodes are less well known in the English-speaking world, however, even as they remain central to France’s own story of the war, from the British destruction of the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in July 1940 (to keep its warships out of German hands) to the epic battle at Bir Hakeim in mid-1942. Perhaps now more familiar to tourists as the name of a Paris metro station, Bir Hakeim saw 3,700 Free French soldiers and their African colonial troops hold an isolated desert fort in Libya against German Gen. Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps for more than two weeks. Fighting against overwhelming odds, their bravery allowed Britain’s Eighth Army to fall back to El Alamein and regroup, marking an eventual turning point in the wider war. Providing the first film with a dramatic 15-minute denouement, the battle proved that de Gaulle’s ragtag movement could fight as a real army, provided a much-needed fillip to Free French morale, and strengthened the general’s position as a legitimate and potentially successful French leader.

Although this is very much a big-budget war movie, much of its power lies, paradoxically, in its intimate portrayal of the quiet complexities of leadership. In the public mind, de Gaulle can often come across as a cartoonish figure, all stubborn resolve, frosty self-regard, and Gallic hauteur. Abkarian’s ramrod-stiff performance is magnetic and provides plenty of evidence of this. But it also offers something more human, portraying with affection de Gaulle’s strange mix of grandeur and loneliness. The first film dwells in particular on his isolation and frequent despair. Arriving in London as a defeated tank division commander and former undersecretary of war, de Gaulle has no army, no money, barely any staff, and little claim to legitimate leadership. His situation is often tragi-comic, as when he tries unsuccessfully to win over members of the French expatriate community at a drinks party, or when he attempts to address a British audience in a packed theater, only to walk off ashamed without saying a word. In one especially memorable scene, he weeps alone in the bath of his small, dingy flat. In many others he is disconsolate, close to losing hope, and tempted to give up.

This most Gallic of films is in fact based on an equally epic book by a British academic: A Certain Idea of France, Julian Jackson’s 900-page biography, published in 2018. Reviewing it in the New Yorker, Adam Gopnik dwelt on the crippling weakness de Gaulle faced in 1940, and how he ultimately managed to think his way out of it via a mixture of imagination, self-belief, and obstinacy. De Gaulle depended “more on theatrical élan than did pretty much any other public man of his century,” as Gopnik put it. “No one has ever played a weaker hand more compellingly. His life was one long brilliant bluff.”

It is this vulnerability, rather than the more familiar image of pigheaded strength, that likely appealed to French audiences, prompting a reassessment of his traditionally unbending image and the controversial Gaullist legacy it inspired. For all that, the film is also huge fun. Its action sequences are slickly executed and, unusually for a European production, come with plenty of exuberant, Hollywood-style explosions. But it works as entertainment above all because at its center is the double act of de Gaulle and Churchill, played by Simon Russell Beale, easily the best of the many actors who have attempted the role.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films

The two men are endlessly frustrated by one another and an obvious study in contrasts: one reserved, austere, and abstemious, the other impulsive, theatrical, and alcoholic. Yet each recognizes in the other a wartime leader fighting to save his nation against massive odds, creating a certain fondness and clear mutual regard. Among their many fine scenes is a comic row involving translation. De Gaulle speaks poor English; Churchill’s French is comical but serviceable. As they argue, both men hear their respective interpreters diplomatically softening their words. Each leader throws his man out of the room in turn, preferring to fight out their differences in broken language. The grudging but sincere warmth between the two both humanizes the complexities of wartime leadership and provides the film’s emotional heart.

Some critics have accused director Baudry of playing fast and loose with history, mixing invented characters with historical leaders, among other sins against accuracy. Jackson, who acted as a consultant on the production, has written warmly in its defense: “My pavlovian historical pedantry – ‘no that is wrong, it didn’t happen like that’, ‘you have these events in the wrong order’, etc – was quickly slapped down with the reminder that this was a film not a documentary.”

The film’s very French portrayal of the United States, with a Machiavellian President Franklin D. Roosevelt cast as a chief villain, is one obvious area of potential historical dispute. But it also provides the film with its drama. Curiously, Adolf Hitler is never seen and barely even mentioned, while few German soldiers even appear. Instead, the real antagonist is Roosevelt’s Washington, and the U.S. president’s mounting frustration with an upstart French exile who contributes little manpower to the war effort yet irritatingly demands to be treated as an equal and a great power. In this sense it has something in common with zombie movies, where the greatest danger often comes less from the outside menace and more from potential betrayal within the group of humans struggling to survive.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films

In Roosevelt’s eyes, France had forfeited any claim to great-power status, while de Gaulle himself was merely an arrogant annoyance and obstacle to his plans. This broader threat to French survival is embodied in a plan to create the Allied Military Government of Occupied Territories (AMGOT), which the film presents as a U.S. scheme to permanently dismantle and divide the country. In this vision, a liberated France would be run by U.S. and British administrators, much as occupied Germany later was. That AMGOT was never the fully formed plan for France the film suggests is almost beside the point. In one memorable scene, Churchill is shown a future map of Europe in which France has vanished, carved up into a “New Wallonia” and other invented entities. In an act of covert friendship, he leaks it to de Gaulle; a rare act of British solidarity with the French over the Americans.

As exaggerated as the film’s version of the AMGOT plan may be—and Jackson concedes it is somewhat overplayed—the question of how to deal with a powerful United States runs throughout the film, giving it its most obvious modern resonance. In part this reflects a traditional and enduring Franco-British divide, with France seeking self-sufficiency and sovereignty while Britain prefers proximity and access to Washington.

To distract from runaway protests, the French president is making a show of independence on the world stage.

The film’s ideas have poisoned military thinking for centuries.

On the eve of D-Day in June 1944, for instance, de Gaulle’s demands over his forces’ role in the coming liberation of France prompt another giant bust-up with Churchill, and one especially memorable exchange, recounted in de Gaulle’s own highly readable memoirs. “”Every time we have to choose between Europe and the open seas, we shall always choose the open seas,”” he recalls Churchill declaring. “”Every time I have to choose between you and Roosevelt, I shall always choose Roosevelt.”” From Churchill’s point of view, this was entirely sensible; Britain had no obvious alternative to a superpower’s existential support, and it would have been foolish to side with an exile liberation army possessing no resources of its own. Nonetheless, it was a line de Gaulle would go on to quote throughout his life: an emblem of British perfidy and deference to Washington.

Late in the second film, in a scene set in November 1944, de Gaulle sounds out Churchill on a deeper Anglo-French alliance. Churchill declines because Britain must stay close to Washington. The portrayal feels both enduring but also clearly modern, depicting two exhausted European powers facing common adversity but still quite unable to choose to be full partners with one another.

More than anything, the film brings to mind the modern predicament of embattled and weakened middle powers, trying to find their way in a world dominated by far larger and more chaotic forces. During World War II, Britain and France both still thought of themselves as great powers—in de Gaulle’s case almost absurdly so, given his limited circumstances. Yet both clearly lived at the mercy of others, be they Hitler’s marauding armies or the caprice of an indispensable but overbearing U.S. ally.

Today European nations face a version of the same bind, struggling to rebuild sovereignty in a world dominated by superpowers increasingly willing to coerce and threaten them. The message of the film is clearly a comfortable one for French audiences: France was right all along about untrustworthy Americans, and about the need for strength and independence rather than reliance on potentially unreliable U.S.-led institutions like NATO. Nonetheless, here de Gaulle offers modern Europeans clear lessons on how to counteract weakness, via a mixture of political imagination, risk-taking, and—above all—a willingness to stand up to U.S. power from time to time.

What most people understand as “Gaullist” policies are increasingly common far beyond France as our geopolitical order frays, not least intrusive industrial policies aimed at technological self-sufficiency. Ben Judah, a British author and former political advisor, has gone further, proposing a new agenda of “Anglo-Gaullism” inspired by the French leader’s mixture of interventionism and political élan. “[T]he genius of de Gaulle was to re-enchant through storytelling a nation that had utterly lost confidence in itself,” he writes. Europe could clearly use a little more of that Gaullist enchantment today.

It is almost a cliche to contrast the giants of World War II with the slighter figures of our own generation. Yet watching de Gaulle’s struggles, it is hard not to think of the supplication of modern leaders like Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary-general, whose approach to U.S. President Donald Trump was memorably described by Susan Glasser of the New Yorker as “strategic self-abasement.” De Gaulle is often fairly criticized for a grandiose vision of French leadership that far outstripped France’s actual power, leading to unhelpful delusions of national grandeur fed by the vision of its grandest of leaders. Nonetheless, de Gaulle’s obdurate refusal to accept decline—and his determination that France should stand, as he put it, as a nation “in the front rank”—should serve as an inspiration to Europe’s leaders today. This, too, is the lesson of the two excellent films that bear his name: to hold a vision of national power and to will it obstinately into existence, even if only by learning how to play a bad hand well.

#5876. Presidential contender's 'remarkably tone-deaf’ move against Trump triggers parental uproar: 'Unconscionable'

Fox News Digital spoke to Defending Education senior communications director Erika Sanzi about Pritzker’s decision to opt out of a Trump administration tax credit funding Illinois student scholarships through a federal school-choice initiative.

Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, widely believed to have presidential aspirations in 2028, is facing pushback from conservative education and school choice advocates over a move to opt out of a Trump federal scholarship tax credit program. Critics say the decision was made based on politics and not student outcomes.

Pritzker announced Tuesday that the state will opt out of the Trump administration’s Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, refusing to allow Illinois students to receive scholarships funded through the federal school-choice initiative.

In a press release, Pritzker argued that participating in what he labeled a "school voucher program" would siphon money and attention away from public education while subsidizing donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics.

GOV KATHY HOCHUL SIGNS NEW YORK ONTO TRUMP'S SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DESPITE TEACHERS UNION OPPOSITION

"At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education," Pritzker wrote.

"We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics."

Prominent conservative education activists and groups lambasted the move on social media, making the case that opting in takes nothing away from public schools and that Pritzker’s refusal simply blocks Illinois students from receiving privately funded scholarships while sending Illinois taxpayers’ charitable dollars to students in neighboring states.

Many also pointed to abysmal test scores in Illinois and noted that Pritzker is siding with the state's powerful teachers unions.

"It is a remarkably tone-deaf moment from Governor Pritzker, just before Thanksgiving, to deny 1.9 million K-12 students in Illinois access to life-changing educational resources as families are faced with rising costs and an affordability crisis," American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz said in a press release.

"Make no mistake: The Education Freedom Tax Credit could have unlocked needed resources for families and students, but Governor Pritzker chose to let those resources go to other states."

Schools for America Executive Director Jane McEnaney wrote on X, "Imagine being Governor of Illinois and hating Donald Trump more than you care about the educational opportunities of 1.9 million kids."

PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS

Students raising hands while teacher asking them questions in classroom. (iStock)

Pritzker's decision comes after three Democratic governors — New York’s Kathy Hochul, Colorado’s Jared Polis and New Mexico’s Michelle Lujan Grisham — agreed to enter the program, saying it brings millions of dollars in additional educational support to students without taking a single cent from public school or state budgets.

The U. S. Department of Education responded to Pritzker’s press release as well, posting on X that by opting out of the program, Pritzker "just handed scholarship dollars from generous Illinois taxpayers to students in other states instead."

Department of Education official Greg Dolan also weighed in on X, saying "the only true thing in this whole statement from @GovPritzker is his name."

"May it live in infamy for so callously and cruelly turning his back on helping students in need," Dolan added.

Erika Sanzi, senior director of communications at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital in an interview that Pritzker’s move was "unconscionable" and a "slap in the face" to parents, who will still be able to write off the taxes. But the money will not go to programs and resources for their children or other students in their state.

A Department of Education sign is displayed outside of their federal student aid office on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

"You don't have to like the program, but can you at least describe it honestly and accurately?" Sanzi said about Pritzker’s statement. "They smear it as a voucher program because vouchers is the scary word but, like, putting aside the merits of vouchers, it's not a voucher program.

"You can stay in the school you're in and still take advantage of these services. That's not a voucher program. I wish I could tell you I was surprised by Governor Pritzker. I am not, but I do think it's disappointing. And I certainly have seen outcry from families in the state that are just extremely frustrated not only by his decision, but by what he said in relation to his decision."

Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker’s office for comment.

The state's major teachers unions praised Pritzker’s move. Chicago Teachers Union and Illinois Federation of Teachers President Stacy Davis Gates applauded the governor for rejecting what she called "Trump's voucher scheme," arguing that "public dollars belong in public schools" and saying the program would pull money out of public education with "zero oversight."

Illinois Education Association President Karl Goeke similarly thanked Pritzker for rejecting vouchers, calling them a "scam" that sends public money to private schools lacking the same testing standards as public schools.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.
